chapters.title: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation

topics.title: Harappan civilisation: names, culture and sites

learn.hook: Over 4,500 years ago, people from the Indus plains to Gujarat were using the same kind of bricks, seals and weights. How do we even name a world that left no readable writing?
points: The Indus valley civilisation is also called the Harappan civilisation, after Harappa, the first site where it was discovered.

In archaeology, a 'culture' means a group of objects of a distinctive style, usually found together within a specific geographical area and period of time. Harappan seals, beads, weights and stone blades form such a group.
The Mature Harappan phase is dated c. 2600–1900 BCE. Cultures before it in the same area are called Early Harappan; those after it are called Late Harappan.

Early Harappan settlements were generally small, had distinctive pottery, agriculture and pastoralism, and some crafts. A break between early and mature phases is shown by large-scale burning at some sites and abandonment of certain settlements.

Key sites: Harappa and Mohenjodaro (now in Pakistan), Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), Kalibangan (Rajasthan), Rakhigarhi and Banawali (Haryana), Chanhudaro (Sindh), Nageshwar (Gujarat coast), Balakot (Baluchistan coast) and Shortughai (Afghanistan).

example.q: A student finds burnt layers at a site lying between Early Harappan pottery below and Mature Harappan seals above. What does this suggest?
steps: Lower layers are older; upper layers are younger.
Early Harappan material lies below, so it came first.
Burnt layers between them point to destruction or a break.
This matches the break seen at some sites before the mature phase.
example.answer: There was a break, possibly with burning and abandonment, between the Early Harappan and Mature Harappan phases at that site.

learn.reallife: Dholavira in Kutch, Gujarat, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021, so a Harappan city is now as much a part of India's heritage list as the Taj Mahal.

games.title: Long timeline of early Indian archaeology

quiz.q: Why is the Indus valley civilisation also called the Harappan civilisation?
options: Harappa was the first site of this civilisation to be discovered
The word Harappa appears on all its seals
quiz.explain: Archaeologists often name a culture after the first site where it was found. Harappa was the first site discovered.
quiz.mistake: Assumes Harappa was a capital; there is no proof of a capital.

quiz.q: In archaeology, the term 'culture' refers to:
options: A group of objects of a distinctive style found together in a specific area and period
The religion followed by a people
Only the art and music of a people
quiz.explain: An archaeological culture is identified by a set of artefacts of a distinct style that occur together in a region and time.
quiz.mistake: Uses the everyday meaning of culture (art, religion) instead of the archaeological one.

quiz.q: The Mature Harappan civilisation is dated to approximately:
quiz.explain: NCERT dates the Mature Harappan phase to c. 2600–1900 BCE.
quiz.mistake: Picks the Late Harappan or Early Historic period.

quiz.q: Which evidence suggests a break between the Early Harappan and Mature Harappan phases at some sites?
options: Large-scale burning and abandonment of some settlements
Writing changing from right-to-left to left-to-right
quiz.explain: At some sites, burnt layers and abandonment mark a break before the mature phase began.
quiz.mistake: Brings in features (iron, coins) of much later periods.

quiz.q: Which pair of site and present-day location is INCORRECT?
quiz.explain: Kalibangan is in Rajasthan. Shortughai is the Harappan site in Afghanistan.

quiz.q: Which of these was a Harappan site located in Afghanistan?
quiz.explain: Shortughai in Afghanistan lay near the source of lapis lazuli. Balakot and Nageshwar are coastal sites; Banawali is in Haryana.
quiz.mistake: Confuses distant trading outposts with coastal sites.

quiz.q: Which statement about Early Harappan cultures is correct?
options: They came after the Mature Harappan cities declined
They had large planned cities like Mohenjodaro
They existed in the same region before the mature phase and had distinctive pottery
quiz.explain: Early Harappan cultures preceded the mature phase; their settlements were generally small, with no large buildings.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Archaeologists use the term 'Harappan culture' for many sites spread across a large area.
Reason (R): Objects such as seals, beads, weights and baked bricks of a distinctive style are found together at these sites.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The shared set of distinctive artefacts is exactly why the sites are grouped as one culture, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the name comes only from geography, not from shared artefacts.

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in: 'If nobody can read their writing, how do we know all these cities belong to one civilisation?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Shared objects in the same area and time make one culture. Gappu is now an amateur archaeologist!
teach.nudge: Hmm, what kinds of objects do these sites share, and where and when are they found?

topics.title: Subsistence: what the Harappans ate

learn.hook: A burnt grain of barley, smaller than a grain of rice, can tell us what was cooked in a Mohenjodaro kitchen 4,500 years ago.
points: Harappans ate a wide range of plant and animal products, including fish. Archaeologists reconstruct diet from charred grains and seeds studied by archaeo-botanists.
Grains found include wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame. Millets are found at sites in Gujarat. Finds of rice are relatively rare.
Animal bones include cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig; studies by archaeo-zoologists show these were domesticated.
Bones of wild species such as boar, deer and gharial are also found. We do not know if Harappans hunted these themselves or got the meat from other hunting communities.
Bones of fish and fowl are found as well, so food came from farmers, herders, fisherfolk and possibly hunter-gatherers.

example.q: List the groups that may have supplied food to a Harappan city.
steps: Grains and pulses: farmers.
Milk and meat of cattle, sheep, goat: herders/pastoralists.
Fish: fisherfolk.
Wild animals: hunters, maybe other communities.
example.answer: Peasants, pastoralists, fisherfolk and hunter-gatherers (or communities trading meat).

learn.reallife: Just as Gujarat today grows bajra and jowar while Punjab grows wheat, Harappan millet finds come mainly from Gujarat sites.

Rice finds are relatively rare; wheat and barley are common.
Millets have been found at sites in Gujarat.
Millets are reported from Gujarat sites.
They identify charred grains and seeds.
We know for certain that Harappans hunted deer themselves.
It is unclear whether they hunted or obtained meat from hunting communities.
Fish bones have been found at Harappan sites.
Fish formed part of the diet.

quiz.q: Which specialists study ancient plant remains such as charred grains?
quiz.explain: Archaeo-botanists study plant remains; archaeo-zoologists study animal bones.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up plant and animal specialists.

quiz.q: Which grain is relatively RARE among Harappan finds?
quiz.explain: Wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame are common; rice is rare.
quiz.mistake: Projects today's eating habits back onto Harappans.

quiz.q: Finds of millets come mainly from Harappan sites in which region?
quiz.explain: NCERT notes millets are found from sites in Gujarat.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a dry region without recalling the evidence.

quiz.q: Which animals' bones show that the Harappans kept domesticated animals?
options: Cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig
quiz.explain: Bones of cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig indicate domestication.

quiz.q: Why are historians unsure about how Harappans got meat of wild animals like deer and boar?
options: No bones of wild animals have been found
It is unclear whether they hunted themselves or obtained meat from hunting communities
quiz.explain: Wild animal bones are found, but the evidence cannot show who did the hunting.
quiz.mistake: Thinks absence of evidence; in fact the bones exist.

quiz.q: Which of these was NOT among the grains and pulses commonly found at Harappan sites?
quiz.explain: Maize is a New World crop that reached India much later. Lentil, sesame and barley are Harappan finds.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all modern Indian crops existed then.

quiz.q: A case: At a Harappan site, an excavator finds charred barley, fish bones and deer bones in one house. What is the BEST inference?
options: The household was a hunting camp only
The household's food came from varied sources, including farming, fishing and possibly hunting
Barley was grown only for animals
quiz.explain: Mixed remains point to a varied diet drawn from different producers.
quiz.mistake: Over-interprets one type of find and ignores the rest.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Rice was the most common grain at Harappan sites.
Reason (R): Charred grains and seeds help archaeologists reconstruct the Harappan diet.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Rice finds are relatively rare; wheat and barley are common.
quiz.mistake: Projects today's diet back onto the Harappans.

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'How can you know a Harappan's menu if they never wrote recipes?'
teach.praise: Yum! Grains, seeds and bones tell the story. Gappu wants Harappan barley khichdi now!
teach.nudge: Which remains do archaeologists dig up to work out food? Think plants AND animals.

topics.title: Farming technology and irrigation

learn.hook: At Kalibangan, archaeologists found a field ploughed nearly 5,000 years ago, with furrows still visible. A farmer in Rajasthan today might recognise the pattern!
points: Seals and terracotta sculptures show the bull was known, so oxen were probably used for ploughing.
Terracotta models of the plough have been found at sites in Cholistan and at Banawali (Haryana).

At Kalibangan (Rajasthan), a ploughed field was found, associated with Early Harappan levels. It had two sets of furrows at right angles to each other, suggesting two different crops were grown together.

Irrigation was probably needed as most Harappan sites lie in semi-arid lands. Traces of canals were found at Shortughai (Afghanistan), but not in Punjab or Sindh. Water from wells and water reservoirs at Dholavira (Gujarat) was also used.
For harvesting, Harappans may have used stone blades set in wooden handles, or metal tools; archaeologists are still not sure.

example.q: Why do furrows at right angles in the Kalibangan field suggest two crops were grown together?
steps: One set of furrows can be used for one crop.
A second set at right angles creates a grid.
Two crops sown in different directions in one field is a known practice.
So the pattern hints at mixed cropping.
example.answer: Criss-crossing furrows suggest that two different crops were grown in the same field at the same time.

learn.reallife: Rajasthan farmers still grow mustard and gram together in one field; the Kalibangan furrows hint that mixed cropping is a very old Indian practice.

quiz.q: Where was evidence of a ploughed field found?
quiz.explain: Kalibangan in Rajasthan has a ploughed field from Early Harappan levels.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the field with Lothal's dockyard-like structure or Shortughai's canals.

quiz.q: Traces of canals have been found at which Harappan site?
quiz.explain: Canal traces come from Shortughai in Afghanistan; none in Punjab or Sindh.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the largest cities must have had canals.

quiz.q: The Kalibangan field had two sets of furrows at right angles. What does this suggest?
options: Two different crops were grown together
The field was used for horse racing
Only one crop was grown each year
quiz.explain: Criss-cross furrows suggest two crops grown together in one field.
quiz.mistake: Reads the pattern as having no agricultural meaning.

quiz.q: Terracotta models of the plough have been found at:
quiz.explain: NCERT mentions terracotta plough models from Cholistan and Banawali.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up evidence for craft and trade sites with farming evidence.

quiz.q: Which site is known for water reservoirs used to store water?
quiz.explain: Dholavira in Gujarat had water reservoirs.

quiz.q: Why was irrigation probably needed by Harappan farmers?
options: Most Harappan sites are located in semi-arid lands
quiz.explain: Semi-arid conditions meant rainfall alone was not reliable.
quiz.mistake: Gives an extreme reason not supported by evidence.

quiz.q: What is the BEST statement about Harappan harvesting tools?
options: They harvested only by hand without tools
They may have used stone blades in wooden handles or metal tools, but this is uncertain
quiz.explain: Archaeologists are unsure; both stone blades and metal tools are possibilities.
quiz.mistake: Assumes iron was available, which belongs to a later period.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Oxen were probably used for ploughing in Harappan times.
Reason (R): The bull appears on seals and in terracotta sculpture.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Familiarity with the bull, shown on seals and terracotta, is the basis for the inference about oxen ploughing.
quiz.mistake: Treats the reason as unrelated evidence.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Did Harappan farmers just throw seeds and pray for rain?'
teach.praise: Super! Ploughs, oxen and water management. Gappu is ready to farm in Kalibangan.
teach.nudge: How did they break the soil, and how did they get water to the fields?

topics.title: Mohenjodaro: a planned city and its drains

learn.hook: Many Indian cities still struggle with waterlogged streets in the monsoon. Mohenjodaro had covered street drains about 4,500 years ago!
points: Mohenjodaro was divided into two parts: a smaller but higher Citadel (to the west) and a much larger but lower Lower Town (to the east). The Citadel was walled, and so was the Lower Town.
Buildings were built on platforms, which served as foundations. This means the settlement was planned first and then built. Platforms needed an enormous amount of labour.
Bricks, sun-dried or baked, were of a standardised ratio: length four times the height and breadth twice the height (4:2:1). This ratio was used across Harappan settlements.
Streets were laid out in an approximately grid pattern, intersecting at right angles. Drains seem to have been laid out first, and houses built along them.
House drains, carrying waste water, were connected to street drains. Long drainage channels had sumps at intervals for cleaning. Drainage systems are found in smaller settlements too, such as Lothal.

example.q: A Harappan brick is 10 cm high. Using the standard ratio, what are its breadth and length?
steps: Ratio length : breadth : height = 4 : 2 : 1.
Breadth = 2 × 10 = 20 cm.
Length = 4 × 10 = 40 cm.
example.answer: Breadth 20 cm, length 40 cm.

learn.reallife: Smart City projects in India stress planned drainage first. Mohenjodaro's planners seem to have done that long ago: drains first, houses next.

items.text: The Citadel was smaller but ___ than the Lower Town.
Brick ratio length : breadth : height = ___
Streets were laid in an approximate ___ pattern.
House drains were connected to ___ drains.

quiz.q: Mohenjodaro was divided into:
options: A larger, higher Citadel and a smaller, lower Lower Town
A smaller, higher Citadel and a larger, lower Lower Town
A temple town and a port
quiz.explain: The Citadel was smaller but higher; the Lower Town was larger but lower.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the size and height of the two parts.

quiz.q: Why does building on platforms suggest that Mohenjodaro was planned?
options: Platforms were made after houses fell down
Platforms show the city grew randomly
The platforms had to be laid first, so the settlement was planned before construction
Platforms were used only for temples
quiz.explain: Platforms acted as foundations; laying them first means the layout was decided in advance.

quiz.q: A Harappan brick is 12 cm high. What is its length according to the standard ratio?
quiz.explain: Length = 4 × height = 4 × 12 = 48 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the breadth multiplier (2) instead of the length multiplier (4).
steps: Length : height = 4 : 1
Length = 4 × 12 = 48 cm

quiz.q: A Harappan brick has a length of 28 cm. What is its breadth?
quiz.explain: Breadth is half the length (4:2), so 28 ÷ 2 = 14 cm.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 4 and gets the height instead of the breadth.
steps: Length : breadth = 4 : 2 = 2 : 1
Breadth = 28 ÷ 2 = 14 cm

quiz.q: Which feature of Harappan drains made cleaning possible?
options: Drains were open pits inside houses
Drains emptied into the Great Bath
Long channels had sumps at intervals
quiz.explain: Sumps at intervals allowed drains to be cleaned.
quiz.mistake: Imagines drains without any maintenance feature.

quiz.q: Which statement about Harappan drainage is correct?
options: It seems drains were laid out first and houses built along them
Each house threw waste water into the street
Drains were found only at Mohenjodaro
quiz.explain: Planning drains first is suggested; drains are also found in smaller towns like Lothal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks drainage was limited to one city.

quiz.q: Reading a site plan of Mohenjodaro, where would you look for the Great Bath?
quiz.explain: The Great Bath and the warehouse are in the Citadel.
quiz.mistake: Assumes public buildings were in the bigger Lower Town.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Harappan bricks of the same ratio were used at sites far apart.
Reason (R): Brick sizes depended on each family's choice.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true: the 4:2:1 ratio is found across settlements. R is false: standardisation points to common planning, not family choice.
quiz.mistake: Fails to see that standard bricks rule out individual choice.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Was Mohenjodaro just a jumble of mud houses?'
teach.praise: Wow, a planned city with drains! Gappu salutes the Harappan town planners.
teach.nudge: What about the two parts of the city, the bricks, and the drains?

topics.title: Houses, the Citadel and the Great Bath

learn.hook: Imagine a house in Mohenjodaro: you walk in from a lane but cannot see the courtyard from the doorway. Privacy mattered even 4,500 years ago!
points: Many Lower Town houses were centred on a courtyard with rooms on all sides. The courtyard was probably used for cooking and weaving, especially in hot and dry weather.
There were no windows in walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard, which suggests concern for privacy.

Every house had its own bathroom paved with bricks, with drains connected through the wall to the street drains. Some houses had staircases to a second storey or roof. Many houses had wells; Mohenjodaro had about 700 wells.
The Citadel had structures probably used for special public purposes, like the warehouse (only lower brick portions survive; upper wooden parts decayed) and the Great Bath.

The Great Bath was a large rectangular tank in a courtyard with a corridor on all four sides, two flights of steps on the north and south, bricks set on edge with gypsum mortar to make it watertight. Its uniqueness and location suggest a special ritual bath.

example.q: Give two reasons why scholars think the Great Bath had a special, perhaps ritual, purpose.
steps: It is a unique structure, not found elsewhere in that form.
It stands in the Citadel, among public buildings.
It had careful watertight construction and side rooms, one with a large well.
example.answer: Its unique design and its location in the Citadel with other special buildings suggest a ritual bath.

learn.reallife: The idea of a sacred tank survives across India, from temple tanks (kalyani or pushkarini) in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu to ghats on the Ganga.

items.text: The tank was made watertight with bricks set on edge and a mortar of ___.
Two flights of steps led into the tank on the north and ___.
A corridor surrounded the tank on ___ sides.
The Great Bath was located in the ___.

quiz.q: What suggests that Harappan house-builders cared about privacy?
options: No ground-level windows facing streets, and entrances not giving a direct view inside
All houses opened onto the Great Bath
quiz.explain: Blank ground-floor walls and indirect entrances kept interiors private.
quiz.mistake: Imagines features not found at Harappan sites.

quiz.q: About how many wells were there at Mohenjodaro, according to archaeologists?
quiz.explain: NCERT notes Mohenjodaro had about 700 wells.
quiz.mistake: Under- or over-estimates by a factor of ten.

quiz.q: What was used to make the Great Bath watertight?
options: Clay pots set side by side
Bricks set on edge with a mortar of gypsum
quiz.explain: The tank was made watertight by bricks set on edge and gypsum mortar.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Harappan materials with later techniques.

quiz.q: Why do only the lower portions of the Mohenjodaro warehouse survive?
options: The lower parts were brick; the upper parts were of wood and decayed
The upper parts were taken to Mesopotamia
quiz.explain: Brick survives better than wood, which decayed long ago.
quiz.mistake: Assumes deliberate destruction instead of natural decay.

quiz.q: The Great Bath had steps leading into it on which sides?
quiz.explain: Two flights of steps on the north and south led into the tank.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the steps with the corridor, which ran on all four sides.

quiz.q: What was probably the main use of the courtyard in a Harappan house?
options: Cooking and weaving, especially in hot and dry weather
quiz.explain: Archaeologists suggest courtyards were used for cooking and weaving.
quiz.mistake: Assigns a public function to a private space.

quiz.q: A case: Across a lane to the north of the Great Bath was a smaller building with eight bathrooms, four on each side of a corridor. What does this suggest?
options: Bathing was organised and may have had a special purpose linked to the Great Bath
Each family in the city had a room there
quiz.explain: Its closeness to the Great Bath and its many bathrooms suggest organised, possibly ritual, bathing.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the building's relation to the Great Bath.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The Great Bath is believed to have been used for some kind of special ritual bath.
Reason (R): It was a distinctive structure located in the Citadel along with other special public buildings.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Its uniqueness and location in the Citadel are the grounds for the ritual interpretation, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the location gives no clue about function.

teach.ask: Gappu is curious: 'What was so special about the houses and the Great Bath?'
teach.praise: Perfect! Courtyard homes, privacy, bathrooms and a ritual bath. Gappu wants a dip!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu about house design and the special building in the Citadel.

topics.title: Tracking social differences: burials and 'luxuries'

learn.hook: In Egypt, pharaohs were buried with mountains of gold. What did Harappans place in their graves, and what does that tell us?
points: Archaeologists study burials and artefacts to find social or economic differences.

At Harappan burial sites the dead were generally laid in pits. Some pits were lined with bricks. Some graves contain pottery and ornaments, perhaps showing a belief that these could be used in the afterlife.

Jewellery is found in burials of both men and women. In one Harappa burial (excavated in the 1980s), a man had an ornament of three shell rings, a jasper bead and hundreds of micro beads. Some burials had copper mirrors.
Overall, Harappans do not seem to have believed in burying precious things with the dead, so burial differences are not very sharp.

Artefacts are classified as utilitarian (daily-use objects like querns, pottery, needles, flesh-rubbers, made of stone or clay, found everywhere) or luxuries (rare objects of costly non-local materials or complicated technology, such as little faience pots). Faience vessels are found in large cities like Mohenjodaro and Harappa but not in small ones like Kalibangan. Gold was rare and found in hoards.

example.q: A grave has a brick-lined pit with pottery, while another has a plain pit with nothing. What can a historian infer, and what caution is needed?
steps: Brick lining and goods mean more effort and resources.
This hints at differences in status.
But Harappan graves rarely have precious items.
So differences existed but were not extreme.
example.answer: There were some social differences, but the evidence does not show sharp inequality like that in Egyptian royal burials.

learn.reallife: Today, archaeologists at Rakhigarhi in Haryana study skeletons and grave goods with DNA and dating methods to learn about the people buried there.

quiz.q: Archaeologists classify an artefact as a 'luxury' when it is:
options: Rare and made from costly, non-local materials or with complicated technology
quiz.explain: Luxuries are rare objects of costly or non-local material or difficult technology.
quiz.mistake: Treats common daily objects as luxuries.

quiz.q: Which of these is a utilitarian object?
quiz.explain: A quern for grinding grain is a daily-use object; the others are rare or costly.

quiz.q: Where are expensive faience vessels mainly found?
options: In large settlements like Mohenjodaro and Harappa
quiz.explain: They are found in large cities and not in small settlements like Kalibangan.

quiz.q: What does the presence of pottery and ornaments in some graves possibly indicate?
options: A belief that these could be used in the afterlife
That the dead were craftsmen only
That burials were done by Mesopotamians
quiz.explain: Grave goods may reflect beliefs about life after death.

quiz.q: What is the overall conclusion about burials as evidence of inequality among Harappans?
options: Burials prove a rich priestly class ruled
Differences existed but were not sharp, as precious things were rarely buried
quiz.explain: Variation exists (brick-lined pits, some goods) but Harappans did not bury great riches.
quiz.mistake: Goes to an extreme in either direction.

quiz.q: Gold among Harappans was:
options: Rare and found in hoards, so it was precious
quiz.explain: Gold was rare and, like today, valued; it is found mostly in hoards.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gold was common or unknown.

quiz.q: In a burial at Harappa, a man was found with an ornament of three shell rings, a jasper bead and hundreds of micro beads. What does this tell us?
options: The man was a Mesopotamian trader
Ornaments were buried with men as well as women
quiz.explain: This burial shows men too were buried with jewellery.
quiz.mistake: Assumes jewellery was only for women.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Faience pots are considered luxury items.
Reason (R): Faience was difficult to make, and such pots are found mainly in large cities.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Difficult technology and limited distribution are exactly why faience pots are classed as luxuries.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the reason to the classification.

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'How can a pot or a grave tell you who was rich?'
teach.praise: Sharp thinking! Burials and luxury objects reveal differences. Gappu is impressed.
teach.nudge: Which two kinds of evidence help trace social differences?

topics.title: Craft production: Chanhudaro and bead-making

learn.hook: A red carnelian bead from the Indus could end up in a royal grave in Mesopotamia. Its journey began at a tiny town called Chanhudaro.
points: Chanhudaro was a tiny settlement (less than 7 hectares) almost exclusively devoted to craft production: bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making.
Bead materials: stones like carnelian (beautiful red), jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite; metals like copper, bronze and gold; and shell, faience and terracotta (burnt clay).
Beads were made in many shapes: disc, cylindrical, spherical, barrel and segmented. Some were decorated by incising or painting, some had etched designs.

Techniques: nodules were chipped into rough shapes, then flaked into final form; grinding, polishing and drilling completed the process. The red colour of carnelian came from firing the yellowish raw material and beads at various stages. Specialised drills have been found at Chanhudaro, Lothal and Dholavira.

To identify a production centre, archaeologists look for raw material (stone nodules, whole shells, copper ore), tools, unfinished objects, rejects and waste material. Waste is one of the best indicators.

example.q: An excavator finds shell pieces with cut marks, broken bangles and whole shells in one area. Is it a craft workshop?
steps: Whole shells = raw material.
Pieces with cut marks = waste.
Broken bangles = rejects/unfinished objects.
All three together point to production on the spot.
example.answer: Yes, it was probably a shell-working centre, because raw material, waste and unfinished objects are found together.

learn.reallife: Khambhat (Cambay) in Gujarat is still famous for agate and carnelian bead-making, a craft with roots going back to Harappan times.

topics.title: Procuring materials within the subcontinent

learn.hook: Copper from Rajasthan, gold from the south, blue lapis lazuli from Afghanistan: Harappan craftspeople ran a supply chain long before trucks and railways.
points: Harappans got raw materials in many ways. Bullock carts carried goods over land; riverine routes along the Indus and its tributaries and coastal routes were probably also used. Terracotta toy models of bullock carts have been found.

One strategy was to set up settlements near sources: Nageshwar and Balakot near shell sources; Shortughai in far Afghanistan near lapis lazuli (a blue stone); Lothal near carnelian (from Bharuch, Gujarat), steatite (south Rajasthan and north Gujarat) and metal (Rajasthan).
Nageshwar and Balakot specialised in making shell objects such as bangles, ladles and inlay, which were sent to other settlements.
Another strategy was sending expeditions: to the Khetri region of Rajasthan for copper and to South India for gold.

In the Khetri area, archaeologists found evidence of the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture, with distinctive non-Harappan pottery and an unusual wealth of copper objects. Its people may have supplied copper to the Harappans.

example.q: Why would the Harappans set up Shortughai so far away in Afghanistan?
steps: Shortughai lies near sources of lapis lazuli.
Lapis lazuli was a highly valued blue stone.
A settlement near the source made regular supply easier.
example.answer: To secure a steady supply of lapis lazuli from close to its source.

learn.reallife: Today, India's Khetri Copper Complex in Rajasthan (Hindustan Copper Ltd) works the same copper belt that Harappans may have obtained copper from.

topics.title: Contact with distant lands

learn.hook: Clay tablets from Mesopotamia speak of a far-off land called Meluhha that sent carnelian and timber. Many scholars think that land was the Harappan region!
points: Copper was probably brought from Oman, on the southeastern tip of the Arabian peninsula. Chemical analyses show both Omani copper and Harappan artefacts have traces of nickel, suggesting a common origin.
A large Harappan jar coated with a thick layer of black clay has been found at Omani sites, and Harappan objects have been found there too.
Mesopotamian texts from about the mid-third millennium BCE mention contact with Dilmun (probably the island of Bahrain), Magan (perhaps Oman) and Meluhha (possibly the Harappan region).

Products from Meluhha mentioned include carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold and varieties of wood. A Mesopotamian myth says of Meluhha: 'May your bird be the haja-bird' — some scholars think the haja-bird was the peacock.
Meluhha is described as a land of seafarers. Mesopotamian seals show ships and boats, and Persian Gulf seals have been found, suggesting sea trade.

example.q: A Mesopotamian text lists carnelian and timber coming from 'Meluhha'. Why do scholars identify Meluhha with the Harappan region?
steps: The goods listed (carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold, wood) match Harappan resources.
Harappan objects and seals are found in the Gulf region.
Meluhha is called a land of seafarers, fitting coastal Harappan sites.
example.answer: Because the goods and the evidence of sea links match the Harappan region, though the identification is still 'possible', not certain.

learn.reallife: Gujarat's Lothal is being developed as a National Maritime Heritage Complex, recalling India's earliest sea trade with the Gulf.

topics.title: Seals, script and weights

learn.hook: Your online parcel has a barcode; a Harappan sack of goods had a clay sealing. Both said: 'Untouched, from the right sender!'
points: Seals and sealings were used to facilitate long-distance communication. A sack of goods was tied with rope, the knot covered with wet clay, and seals pressed on it. The impression is called a sealing; an intact sealing showed the goods were not tampered with and identified the sender.
The Harappan seal is typically made of steatite (a stone). It often has an animal motif and signs from a script that remains undeciphered.
The script was probably not alphabetic, because it has too many signs: somewhere between 375 and 400. It was written from right to left (wider spacing on the right, cramped on the left).
Inscriptions are short; the longest has about 26 signs. Writing appears on seals, copper tools, rims of jars, copper and terracotta tablets, jewellery, bone rods and even an ancient signboard.

Weights were usually cubical, made of chert, with no markings. Lower denominations were binary (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, … up to 12,800), while higher denominations followed the decimal system. Smaller weights were probably for jewellery and beads; metal scale-pans have been found.

example.q: In the binary series 1, 2, 4, 8, …, what are the next three weights after 8?
steps: Each weight is double the previous one.

learn.reallife: Courier companies and India Post use tamper-proof seals and tracking codes; Harappan sealings did the same job of proving goods were untouched.

topics.title: Ancient authority: who ruled the Harappans?

learn.hook: Same brick ratio from Punjab to Gujarat, same weights, planned cities. Who made all these decisions? Historians still argue!
points: Signs of complex decisions: extraordinary uniformity of Harappan artefacts (pottery, seals, weights, bricks); bricks of standard ratio even though not produced in a single centre; planned settlements; craft production organised in places near raw materials.
Palace and king? A large building at Mohenjodaro was labelled a palace by archaeologists, but no spectacular finds were associated with it.

A stone statue was labelled 'priest-king' because archaeologists were familiar with Mesopotamian history and its 'priest-kings'. Harappan ritual practices are not yet understood, so we cannot know if those who performed them held political power.

Theories: (1) there were no rulers and everybody enjoyed equal status; (2) there was no single ruler but several, such as one each for Mohenjodaro and Harappa; (3) these were part of a single state, given the similarity in artefacts, planned settlements, standard bricks and settlements near raw material sources.
As things stand, the last theory seems the most plausible, as it is unlikely entire communities could have collectively made and implemented such complex decisions.

example.q: Which theory of Harappan political organisation does the uniformity of bricks across distant sites support most strongly, and why?
steps: Bricks were made in many places, not in one factory.
Yet they share the same 4:2:1 ratio.
Such uniformity suggests decisions taken and enforced over a large area.
This fits best with a single state.
example.answer: It supports the single-state theory, since a common authority could enforce such standards.

learn.reallife: The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) sets uniform standards for bricks, cement and more across India today; Harappan standardisation suggests some authority did a similar job.

topics.title: The end of the civilisation

learn.hook: Imagine a city where people stopped using writing, seals and standard weights within a few generations. That is roughly what happened after c. 1900 BCE.
points: By c. 1800 BCE most Mature Harappan sites in regions such as Cholistan had been abandoned.
At the same time, population expanded into new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

In the few Harappan sites that continued to be occupied after 1900 BCE, material culture changed: distinctive artefacts such as weights, seals and special beads disappeared; writing, long-distance trade and craft specialisation also disappeared. House construction techniques deteriorated and large public structures were no longer built. These are called Late Harappan or 'successor' cultures, and show a rural way of life.
Suggested causes include climatic change, deforestation, excessive floods, the shifting and/or drying up of rivers, and overuse of the landscape.

These causes may explain the end of some settlements but not the collapse of a whole civilisation. One explanation is the disappearance of a strong unifying element, perhaps the Harappan state, shown by the vanishing of seals, the script, distinctive beads and pottery.

example.q: Why is 'floods' alone not a convincing explanation for the end of the entire Harappan civilisation?
steps: Floods could ruin settlements near rivers.
But Harappan sites were spread over a vast area with different conditions.
A local cause cannot explain the simultaneous disappearance of seals, script and weights everywhere.
So a wider explanation, like the collapse of a unifying state, is suggested.
example.answer: Floods may explain the abandonment of some sites but not the civilisation-wide loss of seals, script and standard weights.

learn.reallife: Ghaggar-Hakra channels and drying rivers are studied by Indian scientists today using satellite images from ISRO to understand how river shifts affected ancient settlements.

topics.title: Discovering Harappa: Cunningham to Wheeler

learn.hook: Alexander Cunningham held a Harappan seal in his hands in the 1870s but could not tell how old it was. The discovery waited another 50 years!
points: Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), began excavations in the mid-nineteenth century. He used accounts of Chinese Buddhist pilgrims (4th–7th centuries CE) to locate early settlements; his main interest was the Early Historic period.
Harappa did not fit his framework. An Englishman gave him a Harappan seal; he tried to place it in a familiar time-frame and failed to realise how old Harappa was (Report on Harappan seal, 1875).

In the early twentieth century, Daya Ram Sahni found seals at Harappa in layers much older than Early Historic levels; R.D. Banerji found similar seals at Mohenjodaro. In 1924 John Marshall, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley.

Marshall excavated along regular horizontal units measured uniformly throughout the mound, ignoring the site's stratigraphy. So artefacts from different layers were grouped together and their context was lost.

R.E.M. Wheeler, Director-General of the ASI from 1944, corrected this by following the stratigraphy of the mound. Later landmarks: Wheeler at Harappa (1946), S.R. Rao at Lothal (1955), B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar at Kalibangan (1960), R.S. Bisht at Dholavira (1990).

example.q: Why was Marshall's method a problem?
steps: A mound has layers formed at different times (stratigraphy).
Marshall dug in uniform horizontal units regardless of layers.
Objects from different layers got mixed in one unit.
So their date and context were lost.
example.answer: Ignoring stratigraphy mixed up artefacts of different periods, destroying valuable information about context.

learn.reallife: The ASI, founded in Cunningham's time, still protects over 3,600 monuments across India, from Dholavira to the Red Fort.

topics.title: New sites and the problems of interpretation

learn.hook: A small clay figure of a woman with heavy jewellery: is she a goddess, a toy or a household charm? Archaeologists must decide with no label attached!
points: After Partition (1947) the major sites Harappa and Mohenjodaro were in Pakistan. Indian archaeologists explored new areas: surveys in Kutch, Punjab and Haryana added many sites, with Kalibangan, Lothal, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira excavated in India. Explorations continued in Pakistan too.

New techniques and questions: scientific analysis of materials, and studies of plant and animal remains, are used to understand diet, trade and environment; since the 1980s there has been growing international interest.

Classifying finds is a basic step: by material (stone, clay, metal, bone, ivory) and by function. Function is hard to know; archaeologists often compare with present-day objects (e.g. querns) or study the context of the find.

Religion is inferred from objects: terracotta female figurines, heavily jewelled with elaborate head-dresses, were called 'mother goddesses'; rare stone statues of men seated in a standard posture were labelled 'priest-king'; fire altars are reported from Kalibangan and Lothal; seals show a 'unicorn' and a figure seated cross-legged in a 'yogic' posture surrounded by animals, regarded as 'proto-Shiva'; conical stones have been classified as lingas.

Such interpretations often use later traditions. For example, Rudra appears in the Rigveda, but he is not depicted there as Pashupati or as a yogi. So using later texts to explain Harappan objects has limits.

example.q: Why is the 'proto-Shiva' identification of the yogic figure on a seal debated?
steps: The identification relies on later Hindu ideas of Shiva as Pashupati and yogi.
The Rigveda, an earlier text, mentions Rudra.
But Rudra in the Rigveda is not shown as Pashupati or as a yogi.
So the link between the seal and later Shiva is uncertain.
example.answer: Because it projects later religious ideas backwards; even the Rigveda's Rudra does not match the image.

learn.reallife: Archaeologists at Rakhigarhi (Haryana) have used ancient DNA analysis, an example of new scientific techniques changing what we know about Harappans.

quiz.mistake: Labels unfamiliar objects as religious without evidence.

Reason (R): The Rigveda's Rudra is not depicted as Pashupati or a yogi, unlike the 'proto-Shiva' seal.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The mismatch between the earlier text and the seal shows why projecting later traditions backwards is risky.
quiz.mistake: Assumes later traditions always explain earlier objects.

chapters.title: Part I: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies

topics.title: Prinsep, Piyadassi and the power of inscriptions

learn.hook: For centuries people walked past pillars covered in strange letters. In 1838 a mint officer cracked the code, and a forgotten emperor stepped back into history.
points: An inscription is writing engraved on a hard surface such as stone, metal or pottery. It usually records the achievements, activities or ideas of those who commissioned it, and serves as a permanent record.

James Prinsep, an officer in the mint of the East India Company, deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi, two scripts used in the earliest inscriptions and coins. He achieved the decipherment of Asokan Brahmi in 1838.

Most Asokan inscriptions call the king Piyadassi, meaning 'pleasant to behold'. He is also called Devanampiya, 'beloved of the gods'. A few inscriptions name him Asoka, which helped scholars identify Piyadassi with the Asoka of Buddhist texts.

Reading inscriptions gave a new direction to early Indian political history: scholars could link rulers named in inscriptions and coins with dynasties in texts and build an outline of political history.

example.q: A pillar inscription mentions 'Devanampiya Piyadassi'. How did historians conclude this was Asoka?
steps: Buddhist texts describe a great Mauryan king called Asoka.
Most edicts use the titles Devanampiya and Piyadassi.
Some inscriptions also mention the name Asoka with these titles.
So Piyadassi and Asoka were identified as the same king.
example.answer: By matching the titles in inscriptions with the name Asoka found in some inscriptions and in Buddhist texts.

learn.reallife: The Lion Capital of Asoka's pillar at Sarnath is India's national emblem, printed on every rupee note and passport.

quiz.explain: Piyadassi means 'pleasant to behold'; Devanampiya means 'beloved of the gods'.

quiz.explain: Devanampiya is 'beloved of the gods'.

quiz.explain: Readable inscriptions gave a new direction to political history.

quiz.q:

quiz.mistake: Assumes inscriptions are neutral records of everyone.

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: 'Who on earth is Piyadassi?'
teach.praise: Bravo! Piyadassi is Asoka, unlocked by Prinsep's decipherment. Gappu bows to the emperor.
teach.nudge: Who deciphered the script and what do the titles mean?

topics.title: The earliest states: sixteen mahajanapadas

learn.hook: Sixteen big kingdoms and republics jostled for power in north India around 2,500 years ago. Think of it as an ancient IPL with sixteen teams!
points: The sixth century BCE is often seen as a major turning point: early states, cities, growing use of iron, the development of coinage, and new systems of thought including Buddhism and Jainism.

Early Buddhist and Jaina texts mention sixteen states known as mahajanapadas. The lists vary, but names such as Vajji, Magadha, Koshala, Kuru, Panchala, Gandhara and Avanti occur often, showing they were among the most important.

Most mahajanapadas were ruled by kings. Some, known as ganas or sanghas, were oligarchies where power was shared by a number of men, often collectively called rajas. Mahavira and the Buddha both belonged to such ganas. In some, like the Vajji sangha, the rajas probably controlled resources such as land collectively.
Each mahajanapada had a capital city, often fortified. Maintaining these cities, early armies and bureaucracies needed resources.

From c. the sixth century BCE, Brahmanas began composing Sanskrit texts called Dharmasutras, which laid down norms for rulers and other social categories. Rulers were ideally Kshatriyas, advised to collect taxes and tribute from cultivators, traders and artisans. Raids on neighbouring states were seen as a legitimate way to gain wealth.

example.q: How did a gana or sangha differ from a kingdom?
steps: In a kingdom, one king held power.
In a gana/sangha, power was shared by many men called rajas.
Resources like land may have been controlled collectively.
So a gana was an oligarchy, not a monarchy.
example.answer: A gana or sangha was ruled by a group of rajas sharing power, unlike a kingdom ruled by one king.

learn.reallife: Vaishali in Bihar, capital of the Vajji sangha, is often called one of the world's earliest republics; a pillar of Asoka still stands at Kolhua near Vaishali.

Reason (R): They required resources, which were collected as taxes and tribute.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

A is true, but R is false

quiz.mistake: Fails to link expenses with revenue.

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'What exactly is a mahajanapada?'
teach.praise: Spot on! Sixteen states, kings and ganas, fortified capitals and taxes. Gappu is impressed.
teach.nudge: How were they ruled, and what did rulers do to support themselves?

topics.title: Magadha: first amongst sixteen

learn.hook: From Rajgir in the hills to Patna on the Ganga, Magadha's rise is a story of iron, elephants, fertile soil and ambitious kings.
points: Between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE, Magadha (in present-day Bihar) became the most powerful mahajanapada.

Modern historians explain this through several factors: agriculture was especially productive; iron mines (in present-day Jharkhand) were accessible and gave resources for tools and weapons; elephants, an important part of the army, were found in forests in the region; and the Ganga and its tributaries provided a cheap and convenient means of communication.
Early Buddhist and Jaina writers explained Magadha's power through the policies of ambitious, ruthless rulers such as Bimbisara, Ajatasattu and Mahapadma Nanda, and their ministers.

The early capital was Rajagaha (the Prakrit name for present-day Rajgir), a fortified settlement among hills. In the fourth century BCE the capital shifted to Pataliputra (present-day Patna), which commanded routes of communication along the Ganga.

example.q: Why would shifting the capital from Rajagaha to Pataliputra make sense?
steps: Rajagaha was protected by hills, good for defence.
Pataliputra stood on the Ganga.
River routes allowed easier movement of goods and armies.
So Pataliputra suited a growing kingdom that needed communication.
example.answer: Pataliputra commanded routes along the Ganga, better for an expanding state than hill-girt Rajagaha.

learn.reallife: Patna remains Bihar's capital, and Rajgir is now a pilgrimage and tourist town with the Nalanda University campus nearby, linking modern Bihar to ancient Magadha.

topics.title: An early empire: Chandragupta Maurya and the sources

learn.hook: A Greek ambassador, a political manual, rock edicts and Buddhist legends: historians use all of these to piece together the Mauryan empire.
points: The growth of Magadha culminated in the Mauryan empire. Chandragupta Maurya founded it around 321 BCE; it extended as far north-west as Afghanistan and Baluchistan.
His grandson Asoka, arguably the most famous ruler of early India, conquered Kalinga (present-day coastal Odisha).

Sources include archaeological finds, especially sculpture; contemporary works such as the account of Megasthenes, a Greek ambassador to Chandragupta's court, which survives in fragments; and the Arthashastra, parts of which were probably composed by Kautilya or Chanakya, traditionally believed to be Chandragupta's minister.

Later Buddhist, Jaina and Puranic literature, and Sanskrit literary works, also mention the Mauryas. The inscriptions of Asoka on rocks and pillars are often regarded as among the most valuable sources.

example.q: Why is the account of Megasthenes useful but limited as a source?
steps: He was a Greek ambassador who saw Chandragupta's court.
So he gives a contemporary, eyewitness view.
But his work survives only in fragments.
And as a foreigner he might misunderstand things.
example.answer: It is a valuable contemporary account, but it survives only in fragments and reflects an outsider's view.

learn.reallife: The Arthashastra's ideas on taxation and administration are still discussed in Indian management and policy courses, often under the name 'Kautilyan economics'.

topics.title: Administering the Mauryan empire

learn.hook: How do you run an empire from Taxila to Karnataka without phones or trains? The Mauryas used five power centres and a military committee.
points: There were five major political centres: the capital Pataliputra and the provincial centres of Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri, all mentioned in Asokan inscriptions.
Taxila and Ujjayini lay on important long-distance trade routes. Suvarnagiri (literally 'the golden mountain') was possibly important for tapping the gold mines of Karnataka.
Administrative control was strongest in areas around the capital and the provincial centres. Communication along both land and riverine routes was vital for the empire's existence.
Megasthenes mentions a committee with six subcommittees for coordinating military activity: navy; transport and provisions; foot-soldiers; horses; chariots; elephants.
The transport subcommittee arranged bullock carts to carry equipment, procured food for soldiers and fodder for animals, and recruited servants and artisans to look after the soldiers.

example.q: List the six subcommittees mentioned by Megasthenes.
steps: Navy.
Transport and provisions.
Foot-soldiers.
Horses.
Chariots.
Elephants.
example.answer: Navy; transport and provisions; foot-soldiers; horses; chariots; elephants.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways is divided into zones with headquarters, like Mauryan provinces, to manage a vast network from different centres.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How did one emperor manage such a huge empire?'
teach.praise: Masterful! Five centres and six subcommittees. Gappu is applying for a Mauryan job.
teach.nudge: Name the centres and describe the military committee.

topics.title: Asoka's dhamma and the Mauryan legacy

learn.hook: After a war in which a hundred thousand were killed, an emperor carved his regret in stone. Asoka's Kalinga edict is one of history's rarest confessions.
points: Asoka's Rock Edict XIII records that in the eighth year of his reign he conquered Kalinga: about 1,50,000 people were deported, 1,00,000 killed, and many more died. He expressed deep remorse.

Asoka tried to hold his empire together by propagating dhamma. Its principles were simple and universal: respect towards elders; generosity towards Brahmanas and those who renounced worldly life; treating slaves and servants kindly; respect for religions and traditions other than one's own.
He appointed special officers, the dhamma mahamatta, to spread dhamma. Asoka believed dhamma would ensure the well-being of people in this world and the next.

Nineteenth-century historians found the Mauryan empire an exciting discovery; the stone sculpture and the inscriptions seemed to mark a high point. Twentieth-century Indian nationalists found Asoka an inspiring figure.

Yet its limits matter: the empire lasted about 150 years, which is not very long, and it did not cover the whole subcontinent. Control was strongest near the capital and provincial centres and much weaker elsewhere.

example.q: How does Rock Edict XIII show a change in Asoka's thinking?
steps: It records the Kalinga conquest and the huge loss of life.
Asoka says he felt deep remorse.
He then turned to spreading dhamma through officials and edicts.
example.answer: It shows a shift from conquest by war to spreading dhamma, prompted by remorse for the suffering in Kalinga.

learn.reallife: The Ashoka Chakra on India's national flag comes from the dhamma chakra on Asokan pillars, a reminder of the ideals of righteousness and tolerance.

quiz.explain: About 1,00,000 were killed and 1,50,000 deported, according to Rock Edict XIII.

topics.title: New notions of kingship: chiefs, Satavahanas and Kushanas

learn.hook: In the south, chiefs were praised in Tamil poems for giving away wealth. In the north-west, Kushana kings called themselves 'son of god'. Two very different ideas of power!
points: In the far south (Tamilakam), new chiefdoms and kingdoms emerged, including the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas. They were prosperous and stable. We know about them from Tamil Sangam texts, poems that describe chiefs and how they acquired and distributed resources.

A chief is a powerful man whose position may or may not be hereditary. He derives support from his kinsfolk. His functions include performing special rituals, leading in warfare and arbitrating disputes. He receives gifts from subordinates (rather than collecting taxes) and redistributes them. Generally, chiefs had no regular officials or army.

Several kings, including the Satavahanas who ruled over parts of western and central India and the Shakas, a people of Central Asian origin who set up kingdoms in the north-west and west, derived revenues from long-distance trade.

Rulers also claimed high status by identifying with deities. The Kushanas (c. first century BCE–first century CE) ruled from Central Asia to north-west India. Colossal statues of Kushana rulers were installed in a shrine at Mat near Mathura (UP), and similar statues in a shrine in Afghanistan.
Many Kushana rulers adopted the title devaputra, or 'son of god', possibly inspired by Chinese rulers who called themselves sons of heaven.

example.q: Compare a chief with a king.
steps: A chief relied on kinsfolk and gifts from subordinates.
A chief usually had no regular officials or army.
A king collected regular taxes and had a bureaucracy and army.
So a king's power was more institutionalised.
example.answer: Chiefs depended on gifts and kin and lacked officials and armies; kings collected taxes and kept officials and standing armies.

learn.reallife: The Government Museum in Mathura displays a headless statue of the Kushana king Kanishka, a famous example of how rulers projected power through colossal images.

quiz.q: Which Tamil texts describe chiefs and how they acquired and distributed resources?
quiz.explain: Sangam poems describe the chiefs of Tamilakam.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Tamil Sangam literature with Pali Jatakas.

options: They collected land revenue through a bureaucracy

They were appointed by the Mauryas
quiz.explain: Chiefs relied on gifts and kin and usually lacked officials and armies.

quiz.q: The Kushana title 'devaputra' means:
quiz.explain: Devaputra means 'son of god'.

quiz.q: Colossal statues of Kushana rulers were found in a shrine at:
quiz.explain: They were found at Mat near Mathura in Uttar Pradesh.

quiz.q: The Kushana title 'devaputra' may have been inspired by:
options: Roman emperors who called themselves consuls
Chinese rulers who called themselves sons of heaven
quiz.explain: Historians suggest a Chinese inspiration.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a Roman or Indian model.

quiz.q: Which dynasty ruled over parts of western and central India?
quiz.explain: The Satavahanas ruled parts of western and central India.
quiz.mistake: Places a southern or north-western dynasty there.

quiz.q: Which was NOT among the chiefdoms of Tamilakam?
quiz.explain: The Kushanas ruled from Central Asia to north-west India.

quiz.q:

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Both are true, but the practice of Tamil chiefs has nothing to do with the Kushana title.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Were all rulers the same kind of king?'
teach.praise: Royal answer! Chiefs, kings and divine kings. Gappu wants a crown too.
teach.nudge: Explain how chiefs differed from kings, and how the Kushanas projected power.

topics.title: The Guptas, samantas and the Prayaga Prashasti

learn.hook: Harishena wrote that Samudragupta's body was 'most charming, covered with the plenty of the beauty of the marks of hundreds of scars'. Was it history or poetry?
points: By the fourth century there is evidence of several large states, including the Gupta empire. Many depended on samantas: men who maintained themselves through local resources, including control over land, and offered homage and military support to rulers.
Powerful samantas could become kings; conversely, weak rulers might find themselves reduced to subordination.
Histories of the Guptas are reconstructed from literature, coins and inscriptions, including prashastis composed in praise of kings by poets.

The Prayaga Prashasti (also called the Allahabad Pillar Inscription) was composed in Sanskrit by Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta, arguably the most powerful Gupta ruler, nearly 1,700 years ago.
Prashastis give useful information, but historians read them carefully: they are poetic praise meant to glorify the king, and may not be literally true.

example.q: A prashasti says the king defeated every rival and was kinder than any god. How should a historian use it?
steps: Note what it claims: victories, virtues.
Remember the author was a court poet paid to praise.
Check claims against coins, other inscriptions and texts.
Accept what is confirmed; treat the rest as royal ideals.
example.answer: Use it for the king's claims and ideals, but cross-check facts with other sources before accepting them.

learn.reallife: The Allahabad (Prayagraj) Pillar stands inside the Allahabad Fort and carries an Asokan inscription as well as Harishena's prashasti and later inscriptions, a stone 'notebook' of many centuries.

topics.title: A changing countryside: kings, subjects and production

learn.hook: In a Jataka story, a wicked king's subjects all complain: an old woman, cowherds, villagers, even a frog! What did ordinary people think of kings?
points: Ordinary people rarely left accounts, but stories in the Jatakas (written in Pali around the middle of the first millennium CE) and the Panchatantra give clues about how they saw kings.

The Gandatindu Jataka describes the plight of subjects of a wicked king: elderly women, men, cultivators, herders, village boys and even animals suffer. Another story shows people fleeing to the forest to escape heavy taxes. Kings often tried to fill their coffers by demanding high taxes, which peasants found oppressive.

To meet growing demands for taxes, people adopted new ways to increase production. One was the shift to plough agriculture, which spread in fertile alluvial river valleys such as those of the Ganga and the Kaveri from c. the sixth century BCE. The iron-tipped ploughshare turned the soil better.
In the Ganga valley, paddy transplantation (raising saplings and then planting them in waterlogged fields) greatly increased yields, though it was very hard work.

Irrigation through wells and tanks, and less commonly canals, was another strategy. Communities as well as individuals organised irrigation works; powerful men, including kings, often recorded such works in inscriptions. Iron ploughs were not used everywhere: in semi-arid parts of Punjab and Rajasthan they came only in the twentieth century, and hilly tracts used the hoe.

example.q: Compare what a king wanted from subjects with what the subjects wanted, using Jataka stories.
steps: The king wanted higher taxes and tribute.
Subjects wanted protection and fair treatment.
When kings were oppressive, subjects suffered and sometimes fled to forests.
example.answer: Kings sought revenue; subjects wanted relief from heavy demands and fair rule, which created tension.

learn.reallife: Paddy transplantation is still how most rice is grown in Bihar and West Bengal during the monsoon, back-breaking work that boosts yields, just as it did 2,500 years ago.

topics.title: Rural society and land grants

learn.hook: A copper plate gifting a whole village to a Brahmana: thousands of such grants survive. What do they tell us about kings, women and peasants?
points: New technologies did not benefit everyone equally. Early Buddhist texts refer to landless agricultural labourers, small peasants and large landholders. The term gahapati was often used for small peasants and large landholders. The gahapati was the owner, master or head of a household, controlling women, children, slaves and workers.
Tamil Sangam texts mention vellalar (large landowners), uzhavar (ploughmen) and adimai (slaves).

From c. the first century CE, land grants were recorded in inscriptions, some on stone but most on copper plates, often given to religious institutions or to Brahmanas. Land granted to Brahmanas was called agrahara; it was usually exempt from land revenue and other dues to the king, and Brahmanas often got the right to collect these dues locally.

Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II (c. 375–415 CE), married into the Vakataka family of the Deccan. Sanskrit legal texts said women had no independent access to land, but her grant shows she had land which she granted, perhaps because she was a queen and her situation exceptional.

Historians debate land grants: some see them as a strategy by ruling lineages to extend agriculture to new areas; others see them as a sign of weakening political power, as kings tried to win allies by granting land. Grants also give a glimpse of relations between cultivators and the state.

example.q: Why is Prabhavati Gupta's land grant significant for the history of women?
steps: Sanskrit legal texts denied women independent access to land.
Yet her inscription shows she held land and granted it.
This was perhaps because she was a queen.
So texts' norms and actual practice could differ, at least for elite women.
example.answer: It shows an elite woman controlling and granting land, unlike the norms of Sanskrit legal texts.

learn.reallife: Copper-plate land grants are still being found by farmers in Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka and handed to epigraphists of the ASI at Mysuru for reading.

topics.title: Towns, guilds and trade

learn.hook: Black pepper from Kerala was so prized in Rome that historians call it 'black gold'. The towns of early India were busy hubs on the routes that carried it.
points: Many major towns grew along routes of communication: Pataliputra on a riverine route, Ujjayini along land routes, and Puhar near the coast, from where sea routes began. Cities like Mathura were bustling centres of commercial, cultural and political activity.

Most cities were fortified. Rulers and urban elites lived in them. Archaeologists have found fine pottery bowls and dishes with a glossy finish called Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), probably used by rich people, plus ornaments, tools, weapons and figurines of gold, silver, copper, bronze, ivory, glass, shell and terracotta.

By the second century BCE, short votive (donative) inscriptions in many cities record gifts to religious institutions by washing folk, weavers, scribes, carpenters, potters, goldsmiths, blacksmiths, officials, religious teachers, merchants and kings.
Guilds or shrenis were organisations of craft producers and merchants. They probably procured raw materials, regulated production and marketed the finished products.

From the sixth century BCE, land and river routes criss-crossed the subcontinent and reached Central Asia and beyond; sea routes went across the Arabian Sea to East and North Africa and West Asia, and through the Bay of Bengal to Southeast Asia and China. Goods included salt, grain, cloth, metal ores and products, stone, timber and medicinal plants. Spices, especially pepper, and textiles were in great demand in the Roman Empire.

example.q: Compare craft production evidence in Harappan cities with that in early historic cities.
steps: Harappa: craft centres identified by raw material, tools, waste and unfinished objects (e.g. Chanhudaro).
Early historic cities: similar finds plus NBPW and many materials.
Early historic cities also have donative inscriptions naming crafts and guilds (shrenis).
So early historic evidence combines archaeology with written records.
example.answer: Both have archaeological evidence of crafts, but early historic cities also have inscriptions naming craftspeople and guilds.

learn.reallife: Kerala still exports black pepper worldwide; the ancient port of Muziris is being explored through the Muziris Heritage Project near Kochi.

topics.title: Coins and kings

learn.hook: Roman gold coins buried in Tamil Nadu, Kushana coins matching Roman weights: coins are like ancient receipts of global trade.
points: Exchanges were facilitated by coinage. Punch-marked coins of silver and copper (c. sixth century BCE onwards) were among the earliest to be minted and used. Their symbols have been identified with royal families, including the Mauryas, though some may have been issued by merchants, bankers and townspeople.
The first coins to bear the names and images of rulers were issued by the Indo-Greeks, who established control over the north-western part of the subcontinent around the second century BCE.

The first gold coins were issued c. the first century CE by the Kushanas. They were virtually identical in weight to those of contemporary Roman emperors and the Parthian rulers of Iran. Hoards of Roman coins have been found in south India, showing networks of trade.
Tribal republics such as the Yaudheyas of Punjab and Haryana (c. first century CE) issued several thousand copper coins, showing their interest and participation in economic exchange.

The Gupta rulers issued some of the most spectacular gold coins; the earliest are remarkable for their purity. From the sixth century CE, finds of gold coins taper off. Some historians link this to a decline in long-distance trade after the collapse of the Western Roman Empire; others note new towns and networks were emerging, and that coins may simply not have been hoarded.

example.q: Arrange the coin 'firsts' in order and give one feature of each.
steps: Punch-marked coins (c. 6th century BCE): silver and copper with symbols.
Indo-Greek coins (c. 2nd century BCE): first with names and images of rulers.
Kushana gold coins (c. 1st century CE): first gold coins, Roman weight standard.
Gupta gold coins (from 4th century CE): spectacular, pure gold.
example.answer: Punch-marked → Indo-Greek → Kushana gold → Gupta gold.

learn.reallife: The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Museum in Mumbai displays punch-marked and Kushana coins, showing the long story of Indian money from silver bits to the UPI era.

topics.title: How are inscriptions deciphered?

learn.hook: Imagine solving a puzzle by working backwards from today's Bengali letters to 2,000-year-old Brahmi. That is how the code was cracked!
points: Brahmi was used in most Asokan inscriptions. From the late eighteenth century, European scholars, aided by Indian pandits, worked backwards from contemporary Bengali and Devanagari manuscripts, comparing their letters with older specimens.
Scholars sometimes assumed early inscriptions were in Sanskrit, but the earliest were actually in Prakrit. After decades of painstaking work, James Prinsep deciphered Asokan Brahmi in 1838.

Kharosthi, used in inscriptions of the north-west, was read differently. Indo-Greek coins carried kings' names in both Greek and Kharosthi. European scholars who could read Greek compared the letters, e.g. matching the symbol for 'a' in names like Apollodotus.

Reading an edict, epigraphists identify titles (Devanampiya Piyadassi), place names and key phrases, add words in brackets to clarify meaning, and then draw inferences, for instance about Asoka's remorse after Kalinga or the officials he appointed.

Landmarks in epigraphy: 1784 founding of the Asiatic Society (Bengal); 1838 Prinsep's decipherment of Brahmi; 1877 Cunningham publishes a set of Asokan inscriptions; 1888 first issue of Epigraphia Indica; 1965–66 D.C. Sircar publishes Indian Epigraphy and Indian Epigraphical Glossary.

example.q: A coin shows a Greek legend 'BASILEOS APOLLODOTOU' on one side and Kharosthi letters on the other. How does this help decipherment?
steps: Scholars could read the Greek name.
The same name was assumed to be written in Kharosthi on the other side.
Matching sounds to symbols revealed Kharosthi letters.
These letters could then be used to read other inscriptions.
example.answer: The bilingual coin acted as a key: the known Greek name revealed the values of Kharosthi signs.

learn.reallife: The ASI's Epigraphy Branch in Mysuru still reads and publishes newly found inscriptions in Brahmi, Tamil-Brahmi and other scripts.

topics.title: Limits of inscriptions and reconstructing ordinary lives

learn.hook: Inscriptions shout about kings' victories but whisper almost nothing about a farmer's daily meal. How do historians fill the silence?
points: Technical limits: letters may be very faintly engraved, so reconstructions are uncertain; inscriptions may be damaged or have missing letters; and it is not always easy to be sure of the exact meaning of words, some of which were specific to a place or time.
Several thousand inscriptions have been discovered, but not all have been deciphered, published or translated. Many more must have existed but have not survived.

Not everything we consider politically or economically significant was recorded: routine agricultural practices and the joys and sorrows of daily life are rarely mentioned. Inscriptions project the perspective of those who commissioned them.
To reconstruct ordinary lives, historians combine inscriptions with texts (Jatakas, Panchatantra, Sangam poems), coins, and archaeology (houses, pottery, tools, crops).

Timeline: c. 600–500 BCE mahajanapadas, paddy transplantation, punch-marked coins; c. 327–325 BCE Alexander's invasion; c. 321 BCE accession of Chandragupta Maurya; c. 272/268–231 BCE Asoka's reign; c. 185 BCE end of the Mauryas; c. 200 BCE–200 CE Shakas, Satavahanas, Kushanas and Sangam literature; c. 320 CE beginning of Gupta rule; c. 606–647 CE Harshavardhana.

example.q: A historian wants to know what peasants in the Ganga valley ate around 300 CE. Which sources should she use?
steps: Inscriptions rarely mention food, so use them carefully.
Use texts like Jatakas or Sanskrit literature for references to food.
Use archaeology: charred grains, pottery, storage jars.
Combine all and note gaps.
example.answer: She should combine texts and archaeological evidence (grains, pottery) because inscriptions alone say little about daily life.

learn.reallife: Many Indian village histories are now being recorded through oral history projects, because, like ancient inscriptions, official records leave out everyday experience.

topics.title: The Mahabharata as a source and its Critical Edition

learn.hook: Imagine collecting handwritten copies of an epic from Kashmir to Kerala, in a dozen scripts, and comparing them verse by verse. Scholars did it for 47 years!
points: Historians use the Mahabharata, among other texts, to study social history c. 600 BCE–600 CE, especially families, marriage, varna and gender.
In 1919, under the leadership of the Sanskritist V.S. Sukthankar, a team of scholars began preparing a Critical Edition of the Mahabharata. It took 47 years to complete.

They collected Sanskrit manuscripts, written in a variety of scripts, from different parts of the country and selected verses that appeared common to most versions. The result was published in several volumes running into over 13,000 pages.

Two things emerged: there were common elements in the Sanskrit versions across the subcontinent, and there were also enormous regional variations, recorded in footnotes and appendices. These showed the complex processes of transmission of the text over centuries.

Many social history sources were Sanskrit texts written by and for Brahmanas, such as the Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras. They were normative: they laid down how society ought to be, which is not always how it actually was.

example.q: Why did the Critical Edition project record regional variations in footnotes instead of deleting them?
steps: The aim was to find verses common to most manuscripts.
But differences also tell us how the text changed in different regions.
Recording them preserves evidence of transmission and local traditions.
example.answer: Because the variations themselves are historical evidence of how the epic was transmitted and reshaped across regions.

learn.reallife: The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune, where the Critical Edition was prepared, is still a major centre for manuscript research in India.

topics.title: Families, lineages and the ideal of patriliny

learn.hook: The world's longest epic is, at its heart, a family fight over property and power between cousins. Sound familiar?
points: Families were usually part of larger networks of people called relatives or kinfolk. Sanskrit texts use kula for family, jnati for the larger network of kinfolk, and vamsha for lineage.

The Mahabharata is a story of a feud over land and power between two groups of cousins, the Kauravas and the Pandavas, who belonged to the Kuru lineage that ruled the Kuru janapada. The Pandavas finally won.

After that, patrilineal succession was proclaimed. Patriliny means tracing descent from father to son, grandson and so on (matriliny traces descent through the mother). The epic reinforced the idea that patriliny was valuable.

Under patriliny, sons could claim the resources of their fathers (including the throne, in the case of kings) after their death. Most ruling dynasties from c. the sixth century BCE claimed to follow this system.
There were variations: sometimes there were no sons, and brothers or other kinsmen succeeded; in very exceptional cases, women such as Prabhavati Gupta exercised power.

example.q: Why might patriliny have been especially important to elite families?
steps: Elite families controlled land, wealth and sometimes the throne.
Patriliny ensured these passed from father to son within the lineage.
Keeping resources within the male line preserved the family's power over generations.
example.answer: Patriliny kept property and political power within the male line, preserving elite families' wealth and status.

learn.reallife: Indian property law changed in 2005, when the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act gave daughters equal coparcenary rights in ancestral property, a big shift from strict patriliny.

topics.title: Rules of marriage and the eight forms

learn.hook: Who could marry whom? Ancient lawgivers wrote long lists of rules, and listed eight ways of getting married, only some of which they approved.
points: Under patriliny, daughters had no claim to the household's resources; they were married into families outside the kin. This system of marrying outside a unit is called exogamy.
Endogamy means marriage within a unit: a kin group, caste or a group living in the same locality. Polygyny is the practice of a man having several wives; polyandry is a woman having several husbands.
Kanyadana, the gift of a daughter in marriage, was considered an important religious duty of the father.
The Manusmriti, compiled between c. 200 BCE and 200 CE, recognises eight forms of marriage. The first four were considered 'good', while the remaining were condemned.
Historians suggest the condemned forms may have been practised by those who did not accept Brahmanical norms, showing that texts' rules and actual practice differed.

example.q: Classify: (a) a man marrying within his own caste; (b) a woman married into a family outside her kin group; (c) a man with three wives.
steps: Marriage within a unit = endogamy.
Marriage outside the kin group = exogamy.
A man with several wives = polygyny.
example.answer: (a) endogamy, (b) exogamy, (c) polygyny.

learn.reallife: Many Indian communities still follow gotra exogamy rules, avoiding marriage within the same gotra, which shows how old norms continue to shape practice.
