topics.title: Gotras, mothers and Gandhari's advice

learn.hook: A powerful king named himself 'son of Gotami' after his mother. Does that mean mothers were in charge? Not so fast!
points: From c. 1000 BCE onwards, Brahmanas classified people (especially Brahmanas) into gotras. Each gotra was named after a Vedic seer, and all its members were regarded as his descendants.
Two Brahmanical rules: women were expected to give up their father's gotra and adopt their husband's on marriage; and members of the same gotra could not marry.

Satavahana inscriptions show that some wives of rulers had names derived from their father's gotra (such as Gotami and Vasithi), so they retained their father's gotra instead of adopting the husband's. Some wives belonged to the same gotra as their husbands, suggesting endogamy, contrary to the Brahmanical ideal; this may reflect kinship practices in parts of the south.

Satavahana rulers were identified through metronymics (names derived from the mother), e.g. Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani, 'son of Gotami'. Though this suggests mothers were important, succession to the Satavahana throne was generally patrilineal.

In the Mahabharata, Gandhari urged her eldest son Duryodhana to make peace with the Pandavas, warning that greed and anger would ruin him. Duryodhana did not listen, fought and lost: the episode shows a mother's voice, and its limits.

example.q: A Satavahana inscription names a king 'Gotami-puta' and his queen 'Vasithi'. What two conclusions can be drawn?
steps: 'Gotami-puta' means son of Gotami: a metronymic.
So mothers were socially significant in naming.
'Vasithi' comes from her father's gotra: she kept it after marriage.
This differs from the Brahmanical rule of adopting the husband's gotra.
example.answer: Mothers mattered in identity, and queens retained their fathers' gotra, unlike the Brahmanical norm; yet succession stayed patrilineal.

learn.reallife: Many Indian surnames and gotra names, such as Bharadwaj, Kashyap and Vashisht, are still traced to Vedic seers, keeping this old classification alive.

topics.title: The varna order and the 'right' occupation

learn.hook: Ancient lawbooks tried to fix every person's job by birth. Did society actually follow? Historians check the rulebook against real life.
points: The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras set out an ideal social order of four categories, or varnas: Brahmanas at the top, followed by Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras.

Prescribed occupations: Brahmanas were to study and teach the Vedas, perform sacrifices and get them performed, and give and receive gifts. Kshatriyas were to engage in warfare, protect people, administer justice, study the Vedas, get sacrifices performed and make gifts. Vaishyas were also to study the Vedas, get sacrifices performed and make gifts, and to engage in agriculture, pastoralism and trade. Shudras were assigned only one occupation: serving the three higher varnas.

Brahmanas used three strategies to enforce these norms. First, they asserted the varna order had a divine origin, citing the Purusha Sukta of the Rigveda, in which the four varnas emerge from the body of the primeval man, Purusha.

Second, they advised kings to ensure that these norms were followed within their kingdoms. Third, they tried to persuade people that their status was determined by birth, reinforced by stories in the Mahabharata and other texts.
These were norms. Historians compare them with other evidence to see how far they were followed in practice.

example.q: How did the Purusha Sukta help support the varna order?
steps: It describes the four varnas arising from Purusha's body.
This presents the order as divinely created.
Something divine appears natural and unchangeable.
So it gave religious authority to the hierarchy.
example.answer: By presenting varna as divinely ordained, it made the hierarchy seem natural and beyond question.

learn.reallife: The Constitution of India, through Articles 15 and 17, prohibits discrimination based on caste and abolishes untouchability, rejecting birth-based hierarchy.

quiz.explain: The Purusha Sukta describes the varnas emerging from Purusha's body.

quiz.explain: The Dharmasutras assigned Shudras only service to the higher varnas.

options: They are norms that may not reflect actual practice
They have been proved false in every case
quiz.explain: Prescriptive texts state ideals; practice could differ.
quiz.mistake: Goes to an extreme in either direction.

quiz.explain: All three were to study the Vedas; only Brahmanas were to receive gifts.

quiz.q:

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A claim of divine origin gives authority; R explains why the strategy was used.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the purpose of the divine-origin claim.

teach.praise: Sharp and balanced! You explained the norms and how they were enforced. Gappu is impressed.
teach.nudge: What were the varnas, their duties, and the three strategies used?

topics.title: Were kings always Kshatriyas?

learn.hook: The rulebook said kings should be Kshatriyas. Yet Brahmanas, Shakas from Central Asia and families of uncertain origin all ruled. Rules and reality clashed!
points: According to the Shastras, only Kshatriyas could be kings. But many important ruling lineages had different origins.

The Mauryas: later Buddhist texts suggested they were Kshatriyas, but Brahmanical texts described them as being of 'low' origin. The Shungas and Kanvas, the immediate successors of the Mauryas, were Brahmanas.
In fact, political power was effectively open to anyone who could muster support and resources, and rarely depended on birth as a Kshatriya.

The Shakas came from Central Asia and were regarded as mlechchhas (barbarians, outsiders) by the Brahmanas. Yet one of the earliest inscriptions in Sanskrit describes how Rudradaman, the best-known Shaka ruler (c. second century CE), rebuilt the Sudarshana lake.

The Satavahana ruler Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani claimed to be a unique Brahmana (eka bamhana) and a destroyer of the pride of Kshatriyas. He also claimed to have prevented intermarriage among the four varnas, yet entered into a marriage alliance with the kin of Rudradaman, a Shaka.

example.q: Use Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani to show the gap between norms and practice.
steps: He claimed to uphold the varna order and prevent intermarriage.
He called himself a unique Brahmana.
Yet he made a marriage alliance with the Shakas, considered outsiders.
So political needs overrode the norms he claimed to defend.
example.answer: He claimed to protect the varna order, yet married into a Shaka family, showing practice often departed from norms.

learn.reallife: The Junagadh rock in Gujarat carries inscriptions of Asoka, Rudradaman and Skandagupta on the same boulder, a single stone recording three very different rulers.

A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Both are true: Rudradaman's Sanskrit inscription is early, and Brahmanas did call Shakas mlechchhas. But being called mlechchhas does not explain why Rudradaman used Sanskrit.
quiz.mistake: Assumes any two true statements must be cause and effect.

topics.title: Jatis, guilds and social mobility

learn.hook: Silk weavers from Gujarat migrated to Madhya Pradesh, built a sun temple and some even changed jobs. A 1,500-year-old inscription tells their story!
points: In Brahmanical theory, jati, like varna, was based on birth. But while there were only four varnas, there was no fixed number of jatis.

Whenever Brahmanical authorities encountered new groups (for example, people living in forests such as the nishadas) or wanted to assign a social status to an occupation (such as the goldsmith, suvarnakara), they classified them as a jati. So the jati system was open to new groups.
Jatis that shared a common occupation or profession were sometimes organised into shrenis or guilds.

The Mandasor inscription (Madhya Pradesh, c. fifth century CE) records the history of a guild of silk weavers who originally lived in Lata (Gujarat) and migrated to Mandasor, then known as Dashapura, with their children and kinfolk, having heard of the greatness of the local king.

The inscription says they built a temple to the sun god. It also records that some members took up other occupations, which shows that guild members shared an identity beyond their craft and that occupations were not always fixed.

example.q: What does the Mandasor inscription suggest about the rigidity of occupations?
steps: The guild was defined by silk weaving.
After migrating, some members took up other occupations.
They still shared a common identity as a guild.
So occupation was not strictly fixed by birth for everyone.
example.answer: It suggests occupations could change and that guild identity went beyond a single craft, so the system was more flexible than the norms claim.

learn.reallife: Mandsaur in Madhya Pradesh is today known for its Pashupatinath temple and opium-poppy farming, while Gujarat's silk weaving lives on in Patan's famous patola saris.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: There were four varnas but no fixed number of jatis.

topics.title: Beyond the four varnas: integration, exclusion and Ekalavya

learn.hook: A forest boy taught himself archery by practising before a clay image of his teacher, and was asked to cut off his thumb. Why does this story still trouble readers?
points: Integration: some communities, such as forest dwellers who hunted, gathered or practised shifting cultivation (like the nishadas, to whom Ekalavya belonged), and nomadic pastoralists, were not easily fitted into the varna order. People who spoke non-Sanskritic languages were labelled mlechchhas. Ideas and beliefs were exchanged between these groups and others.

Subordination: Brahmanas classified certain social categories as 'untouchable', declaring activities like handling corpses and dead animals 'polluting'. Those classified as chandalas were placed at the very bottom; the Manusmriti laid down that they live outside the village, use discarded utensils, wear clothes of the dead, dispose of bodies with no relatives, and serve as executioners.

The Chinese pilgrim Fa Xian (c. fifth century CE) wrote that 'untouchables' had to sound a clapper in the streets so that people could avoid seeing them. Xuan Zang (c. seventh century) observed that executioners and scavengers were forced to live outside the city.

In the Ekalavya story, Drona refused to teach Ekalavya, a forest-dwelling nishada. Ekalavya made a clay image of Drona, practised and became an expert archer. Drona then demanded his right thumb as his fee; Ekalavya cut it off and lost his speed. Drona thus kept his word to Arjuna that no one would be better than him.

Another episode: in the forest, Bhima married Hidimba, a rakshasa woman, and they had a son, Ghatotkacha. Stories like these show contact with communities outside the Brahmanical order, though described in Brahmanical terms.

example.q: What message about social hierarchy might the Ekalavya story convey to readers in Brahmanical tradition, and how can a modern historian read it?
steps: Drona refuses an outsider and demands his thumb.
Ekalavya obeys without protest.
The story seems to uphold the idea that skills belong to certain groups.
A historian reads it as evidence of exclusion, and also of how texts justified it.
example.answer: It reflects and reinforces the exclusion of forest groups from elite learning; historians read it critically as evidence of social exclusion.

learn.reallife: Many schools and sports academies in tribal areas of India today, such as Eklavya Model Residential Schools, are named after Ekalavya, reclaiming him as a symbol of talent and determination.

quiz.explain: Drona denies Ekalavya his teaching and takes his thumb, which reflects exclusion. Bhima marries Hidimba and they have a son, Ghatotkacha, which shows interaction with forest people, though told in Brahmanical terms.

topics.title: Gender and property: stridhana and the Manusmriti

learn.hook: Draupadi was staked in a game of dice as if she were property. Could women in early India own property themselves?
points: In the Mahabharata's game of dice, Yudhishthira lost his wealth and then staked and lost Draupadi, which raises questions about whether women were treated as property. Gender was a key factor in access to property.

According to the Manusmriti, the paternal estate was to be divided equally among sons after the death of both parents, with a special share for the eldest. Women could not claim a share of these resources.

Women were allowed to keep the gifts they received at marriage as stridhana (literally, a woman's wealth). This could be inherited by their children, and the husband had no claim on it. However, the Manusmriti warned women against hoarding family property, or even their own valuables, without the husband's permission.

The Manusmriti lists seven means of acquiring wealth for men: inheritance, finding, purchase, conquest, investment, work, and acceptance of gifts from good people. For women it lists six: what was given before the nuptial fire, in the bridal procession, as a token of love, and by her brother, mother and father; plus subsequent gifts and what an 'affectionate' husband gave.
Elite women such as Prabhavati Gupta had access to land, but in general, land, cattle and money were controlled by men, so social differences between men and women were sharpened.

example.q: Using the Manusmriti, compare how men and women could acquire wealth.
steps: Men had seven means including inheritance, purchase, conquest, investment and work.
Women had six means, all essentially gifts from family or husband.
Women could not inherit the paternal estate.
So women's economic independence was limited.
example.answer: Men could inherit, earn and conquer; women mainly received gifts (stridhana), so women had far less control over resources.

learn.reallife: Today, the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 gives daughters equal rights in ancestral property, a sharp contrast with the Manusmriti's rules.

topics.title: Varna, wealth, Buddhist critiques and the social contract

learn.hook: What if kings were not chosen by gods, but by people tired of quarrelling over rice? A Buddhist story suggested exactly that!
points: According to Brahmanical texts, access to wealth was linked to varna: Shudras could only serve, while Brahmanas and Kshatriyas were, in theory, the wealthiest. Yet texts also mention poor Brahmanas and wealthy members of other groups.

Buddhists recognised social differences but did not regard them as natural or inflexible. They rejected the idea of claims to status on the basis of birth. In a story from the Majjhima Nikaya, a disciple of the Buddha, Kachchana, tells King Avantiputra that a rich Shudra could have Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas as his servants, and that wrongdoers of any varna would suffer the same fate, so birth does not decide worth.

In the Tamil Sangam anthologies, chiefs were patrons of bards and poets, and their generosity in distributing wealth was praised. This shows an alternative ideal where sharing wealth, not hoarding it, brought status.

The Sutta Pitaka has a myth explaining kingship: as greed, vindictiveness and deceit grew, people decided to select a being who would censure and punish wrongdoers, and to give him a share of rice in return. He was chosen by the whole people and called mahasammata, the great elect.
This suggests kingship was based on human choice, with taxes as payment for services: a 'social contract'. It contrasts with the Brahmanical idea that the social order was divinely ordained.

example.q: How did the Buddhist explanation of kingship differ from the Brahmanical view?
steps: Brahmanical view: social order, including kings and varnas, is divinely ordained.
Buddhist myth: people chose a ruler (mahasammata) to settle disputes.
The ruler was paid with a share of rice.
So authority rests on human choice and can be questioned.
example.answer: Buddhists saw kingship as a human institution based on choice and exchange (a social contract), not as a divine order.

learn.reallife: In a democracy like India, rulers are chosen through elections and paid through taxes, an idea that echoes the Buddhist mahasammata story.

topics.title: Handling texts: language, content, authors and dates

learn.hook: The Mahabharata grew from a war story of perhaps 10,000 verses to about 1,00,000 verses. How does a story grow ten times bigger?
points: Language: the Mahabharata's Sanskrit is far simpler than that of the Vedas or the prashastis, so it was probably widely understood.

Content: historians classify it into narrative sections containing stories and didactic sections containing prescriptions about social norms. The Mahabharata is often described as itihasa, meaning 'thus it was', a history.

Authors: it is traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa. Historians think the original story was probably composed by charioteer-bards called sutas, who accompanied Kshatriya warriors to the battlefield and composed poems celebrating their victories. These circulated orally.

From the fifth century BCE, Brahmanas took over the story and began to write it down. Between c. 200 BCE and 200 CE, the worship of Vishnu grew and Krishna came to be identified with Vishnu. Between c. 200 and 400 CE, large didactic sections resembling the Manusmriti were added.

Composition spread over a long period (c. 500 BCE onwards, up to c. 400 CE). The text grew from perhaps less than 10,000 verses to about 1,00,000 verses. Textual timeline: Rigveda (c. 1500–1000 BCE) → later Vedic texts (c. 1000–500 BCE) → Dharmasutras and early Buddhist and Jaina texts (c. 500–200 BCE) → Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE–200 CE) → Puranas (compiled from c. 200 CE onwards).

example.q: Why do historians call the Mahabharata a text 'composed over centuries'?
steps: The story began as oral poems of sutas.
Brahmanas began writing it down from the fifth century BCE.
Krishna's identification with Vishnu was added c. 200 BCE–200 CE.
Didactic sections were added c. 200–400 CE.
So different layers come from different times.
example.answer: Because it has layers added by different composers at different times, growing from under 10,000 to about 1,00,000 verses.

learn.reallife: Doordarshan's Mahabharat (1988–90) and many later TV and web adaptations show how the epic keeps growing and being retold for new audiences.

quiz.explain: Later additions like the didactic sections are an example of layering, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the text was composed at one time.

topics.title: Hastinapura and Draupadi's marriage: searching for convergence

learn.hook: Was the Hastinapura of the epic a real city? An archaeologist dug in a village with that very name in the 1950s to find out.
points: Historians search for convergence between texts and archaeology. Between 1951 and 1952, the archaeologist B.B. Lal excavated at a village named Hastinapura in Meerut (Uttar Pradesh).

He found evidence of five occupational levels. The second phase (c. twelfth to seventh centuries BCE) had houses with mud walls and mud-brick; the third phase (c. sixth to third centuries BCE) had houses of mud-brick and burnt bricks, soakage jars and brick drains, and terracotta ring wells.
Whether this was the Hastinapura of the epic remains uncertain; the similarity of names may be a coincidence. The descriptions in the epic may have been added later when cities flourished.
Draupadi's marriage to the five Pandavas (polyandry) is a central episode. The epic itself offers explanations, but historians suggest others.

Some suggest polyandry may have been prevalent among ruling elites at some point, and fell out of favour among Brahmanas who reworked the text. Some note that polyandry existed in the Himalayan region. Others suggest that a shortage of women during times of warfare may have led to it.

example.q: Why can't historians simply say B.B. Lal found the Hastinapura of the Mahabharata?
steps: The village has the same name.
Its remains date to the right broad period.
But no inscription links it to the Kauravas.
Epic descriptions may come from a later time.
So the identification remains uncertain.
example.answer: Because a shared name and broad date are not proof; the match between text and site is uncertain.

learn.reallife: Hastinapur in Meerut district is now home to Jain temples and a wildlife sanctuary; in 2020 it was announced as one of five iconic archaeological sites for development.

topics.title: A dynamic text: the Mahabharata through the ages

learn.hook: A Bengali writer retold one episode from the point of view of a nishada woman who died in the fire meant for the Pandavas. The epic speaks back!
points: The Mahabharata did not stop growing after the Sanskrit versions. Over centuries, versions were written in a variety of languages through an ongoing dialogue between peoples, communities and those who wrote the texts.
Many local stories, which originated in specific regions or circulated among certain people, found their way into the epic. At the same time, the central story was often retold in different ways.
Episodes were depicted in sculpture and painting, and provided themes for a wide range of performing arts: plays, dance and other kinds of narration.

The Bengali writer Mahasweta Devi wrote 'Kunti O Nishadi', a short story in which a nishada woman questions Kunti about the burning of the lac house, in which a nishada woman and her five sons died so that the Pandavas could escape. Such retellings explore voices left out of the original.
This is why the Mahabharata is called a dynamic text: it kept changing in dialogue with changing social practices and new audiences.

example.q: Give three reasons why the Mahabharata is called a dynamic text.
steps: It was written in many regional languages.
Local stories were absorbed and the central story retold differently.
It was expressed in sculpture, painting, theatre and dance.
Modern authors retell it from new perspectives.
example.answer: Because it kept changing through regional versions, art and performance, and retellings that question the original.

learn.reallife: From Kerala's Kathakali to Pandavani storytelling in Chhattisgarh by Teejan Bai, Mahabharata episodes are performed across India, each region adding its own flavour.

topics.title: A glimpse of Sanchi and its preservation

learn.hook: In the nineteenth century, French officials wanted to ship Sanchi's eastern gateway to Paris. Thanks to the rulers of Bhopal, it is still standing in Madhya Pradesh!
points: Sanchi, near Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh, has one of the best-preserved Buddhist stupas. It is among the most important surviving evidence of early Buddhism.
In the nineteenth century, the rulers of Bhopal, Shahjehan Begum and her successor Sultan Jehan Begum, provided money for the preservation of the ancient site.

The French sought Shahjehan Begum's permission to take away the eastern gateway for display in France. Both the French and the English were eventually satisfied with carefully prepared plaster-cast copies, and the originals remained at Sanchi.
John Marshall dedicated his important volumes on Sanchi to Sultan Jehan Begum. She funded the museum built there, the guesthouse where Marshall lived and wrote, and the publication of the volumes.
Sanchi was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1989.

example.q: Why do historians praise the role of the Begums of Bhopal?
steps: They funded preservation of the site.
They supported a museum and a guesthouse for scholars.
They funded publication of Marshall's volumes.
Their support kept the original gateways at Sanchi.
example.answer: Their funds and decisions helped preserve Sanchi where it stood and supported scholarship on it.

learn.reallife: Sanchi's stupa and gateway appear on the back of India's ₹200 note, issued in 2017, showing its place in national heritage.

topics.title: Sacrifices and debates: the background

learn.hook: Around 2,500 years ago, thinkers in Greece, China, Iran and India were all asking the big questions about life. It was a global age of ideas!
points: The mid-first millennium BCE is a turning point in world history: thinkers such as Zarathustra (Iran), Kong Zi (China), Socrates, Plato and Aristotle (Greece), and Mahavira and Gautama Buddha (India) emerged.

The Rigveda (compiled c. 1500–1000 BCE) has hymns praising Agni (god of fire), Indra (a warrior deity) and Soma (a plant from which a special drink was prepared). Sacrifices were performed to ask for cattle, sons, good health and long life. Elaborate sacrifices like the rajasuya and ashvamedha were performed by chiefs and kings who depended on Brahmana priests.

In the sixth century BCE and after, many people asked new questions. Ideas in the Upanishads show interest in the meaning of life, the possibility of life after death and rebirth. Were rebirths due to past actions (karma)? Thinkers also discussed the atman (individual soul) and the brahman (universal soul), and some questioned the value of sacrifices.

Buddhist texts mention as many as 64 sects or schools of thought. Teachers travelled from place to place, debating with one another and with lay people, in the kutagarashala (literally a hut with a pointed roof) or in groves where travelling mendicants halted.

In a Buddhist text, Makkhali Gosala, a fatalist (Ajivika), argues that everything is predetermined, while Ajita Kesakambalin, a materialist, argues that a person is made of four elements that dissolve at death, so nothing survives. Both speak to King Ajatasattu of Magadha. Upanishadic thinkers, by contrast, explored the atman, brahman, karma and rebirth.

example.q: How was Upanishadic thought different from that of fatalists and materialists?
steps: Upanishads: the atman and brahman exist; actions (karma) shape rebirth.
Fatalists (Makkhali Gosala): everything is predetermined; effort cannot change it.
Materialists (Ajita Kesakambalin): nothing survives death; no next world.
So Upanishads accepted a soul and moral causation; the others denied either free effort or any afterlife.
example.answer: Upanishadic thinkers believed in the soul, karma and rebirth, whereas fatalists denied that effort mattered and materialists denied any life after death.

learn.reallife: India's tradition of public debate, shastrartha, lives on in TV debates and college debating societies, where rival views are argued before an audience.

topics.title: Beyond worldly pleasures: the message of Mahavira

learn.hook: Some Jaina monks cover their mouths with cloth so they do not harm tiny insects while breathing. That is ahimsa taken very seriously!
points: The basic philosophy of the Jainas existed before Vardhamana Mahavira. According to Jaina tradition, Mahavira was preceded by 23 other teachers, the tirthankaras, literally 'those who guide men and women across the river of existence'. Mahavira is the 24th.
The most important idea in Jainism is that the entire world is animated: even stones, rocks and water have life.
Non-injury (ahimsa) to living beings, especially to humans, animals, plants and insects, is central to Jaina philosophy.

The cycle of birth and rebirth is shaped through karma. Asceticism and penance are required to free oneself from the cycle of karma; this is possible only by renouncing the world, so monastic existence is necessary for salvation.

Jaina monks and nuns took five vows: to abstain from killing, stealing and lying; to observe celibacy; and to abstain from possessing property. Jainism spread to many parts of India, and Jaina scholars produced literature in Prakrit, Sanskrit and Tamil, preserved in libraries attached to temples.

example.q: Why would a Jaina monk avoid walking on grass and sweep the path ahead?
steps: Jainas believe the whole world is animated, even plants and tiny creatures.
Ahimsa forbids injury to any living being.
Sweeping and careful walking avoid harming small beings.
So the practice follows from the belief that all things have life.
example.answer: Because Jainism holds that all things are alive and requires ahimsa towards every living being.

learn.reallife: Shravanabelagola in Karnataka hosts the Mahamastakabhisheka of the 57-foot Gommateshwara (Bahubali) statue every twelve years, drawing pilgrims from across India.

topics.title: The Buddha and the quest for enlightenment

learn.hook: A prince saw an old man, a sick man and a corpse on a single chariot ride, and walked away from his palace forever.
points: Siddhartha, also known as Gotama, was the son of a chief of the Sakya clan. He had a sheltered upbringing in the palace.

One day he persuaded his charioteer to take him into the city. He saw an old man, a sick man and a corpse, and was deeply shocked to realise that the human body would decay and die. He also saw a homeless mendicant who seemed to have come to terms with old age, disease and death, and found peace.

Siddhartha left the palace in search of truth. He explored several paths, including bodily mortification, which nearly killed him. Abandoning these extreme methods, he meditated for several days and attained enlightenment. He came to be known as the Buddha, the Awakened One or the Enlightened One.
For the rest of his life he taught dhamma, the path of righteous living. He passed away at Kusinara (Kusinagara); this is called his mahaparinibbana.
Historians reconstruct the Buddha's teachings mainly from stories found in the Sutta Pitaka, which developed from his oral teachings.

example.q: Arrange the key events of the Buddha's life and link each to a place.
steps: Birth: Lumbini.
Enlightenment: Bodh Gaya.
First sermon: Sarnath.
Mahaparinibbana: Kusinagara.
example.answer: Lumbini → Bodh Gaya → Sarnath → Kusinagara.

learn.reallife: The Indian government promotes a Buddhist Circuit linking Bodh Gaya (Bihar), Sarnath and Kushinagar (UP) and Lumbini (Nepal); Kushinagar got an international airport in 2021.

topics.title: The teachings of the Buddha

learn.hook: 'Be lamps unto yourselves,' the Buddha told his followers. No god or priest would do the work for you: liberation was in your own hands.
points: According to Buddhist philosophy, the world is transient (anicca) and constantly changing; it is also soulless (anatta), as there is nothing permanent or eternal in it. Within this transient world, sorrow (dukkha) is intrinsic to human existence.
By following the path of moderation between severe penance and self-indulgence, human beings can rise above these worldly troubles.

In the earliest forms of Buddhism, whether or not god existed was irrelevant. The Buddha regarded the social world as a human creation rather than of divine origin, and advised kings and gahapatis to be humane and ethical. Individual effort was expected to transform social relations.
The Buddha emphasised individual agency and righteous action as the means to escape the cycle of rebirth and attain nibbana, literally the extinguishing of the ego and desire.

To the wealthy householder Sigala, the Buddha advised that a master should look after servants by assigning work according to their strength, supplying food and wages, tending them in sickness, sharing delicacies and granting leave; servants, in return, should work well and speak well of the master.

example.q: Summarise the central teachings of Jainism and Buddhism side by side.
steps: Jainism: all things are alive; ahimsa; freedom from karma through renunciation and penance; five vows.
Buddhism: world is anicca and anatta; dukkha is intrinsic; middle path; nibbana through individual effort.
Both reject Vedic sacrifices and stress conduct.
Both have monastic orders.
example.answer: Jainism stresses ahimsa and asceticism; Buddhism stresses the middle path and nibbana; both emphasise right conduct and renunciation.

learn.reallife: Modern ideas of fair workplace treatment, like paid leave, fair wages and health care, echo the Buddha's advice to Sigala about how masters should treat workers.

topics.title: Followers of the Buddha: the sangha and the Tipitaka

learn.hook: The Buddha's own foster mother became the first Buddhist nun, and women's poems from that time survive in a collection called the Therigatha!
points: The Buddha founded a sangha, an organisation of monks who also became teachers of dhamma. They lived simply, with only the essential requisites, including a bowl to receive food once a day from lay followers. As they lived on alms, they were called bhikkhus; women were called bhikkhunis.

Initially only men were allowed into the sangha. Later women came in: according to Buddhist texts, through the mediation of Ananda, one of the Buddha's dearest disciples, the Buddha's foster mother Mahapajapati Gotami became the first woman ordained as a bhikkhuni.

Many women became teachers of dhamma and went on to become theris, respected women who had attained liberation. The Therigatha, a unique Buddhist text that is part of the Sutta Pitaka, is a collection of verses composed by bhikkhunis.

Followers came from many social groups: kings, wealthy men and gahapatis, and humbler folk such as workers, slaves and craftspeople. Within the sangha all were regarded as equal; internal functioning followed the traditions of ganas and sanghas, reaching consensus through discussion and, if that failed, by vote.

The Buddha's teachings were compiled after his death at a council of senior monks at Vesali (Vaishali). They were arranged in the Tipitaka (three baskets): the Vinaya Pitaka (rules for the sangha), the Sutta Pitaka (teachings of the Buddha) and the Abhidhamma Pitaka (philosophical matters). Buddhism spread rapidly, appealing to people dissatisfied with existing practices, with its stress on conduct, metta (fellow feeling) and karuna (compassion).

example.q: Why did Buddhism appeal to so many people from different backgrounds?
steps: It valued conduct over claims of superiority by birth.
It stressed metta and karuna, especially for the weak.
All were equal within the sangha.
It offered a path to people confused by rapid social change.
example.answer: Its emphasis on conduct, compassion and equality within the sangha attracted people of many social groups.

learn.reallife: Vaishali in Bihar, where the council of senior monks met, is today an important stop on India's Buddhist pilgrimage circuit, visited by monks and tourists from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Japan and beyond.

topics.title: Why and how were stupas built?

learn.hook: Ivory carvers of Vidisha paid for part of one of Sanchi's gateways. Ordinary donors' names are still carved on its railings!
points: Since early times, people regarded certain places as sacred: trees, rocks or places of natural beauty, often with shrines called chaityas. Places associated with the Buddha's life, such as Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kusinagara, also became sacred. Asoka erected a pillar at Lumbini to mark his visit.

Stupas were mounds in which relics of the Buddha, such as his bodily remains or objects he used, were buried. Because they contained relics regarded as sacred, the entire stupa came to be venerated as an emblem of the Buddha and Buddhism.

According to the Buddhist text Ashokavadana, Asoka distributed portions of the Buddha's relics to every important town and ordered stupas to be built over them. By the second century BCE, stupas at Bharhut, Sanchi and Sarnath had been built.

Inscriptions on railings and pillars record donations. Some were made by kings such as the Satavahanas; others by guilds, such as the ivory workers who financed part of one of the gateways at Sanchi. Hundreds of women and men, bhikkhus and bhikkhunis, donated and recorded their names, places, occupations and relatives' names.
Worshippers entered through the eastern gateway and walked around the mound in a clockwise direction, keeping it on the right, imitating the sun's course. This is pradakshina (circumambulation).

example.q: Why did people of many backgrounds donate to stupas and record their names?
steps: Stupas held the Buddha's relics and were sacred.
Donating was a way to earn merit.
Names, places and occupations recorded their piety and status.
So many people, not just kings, felt part of building the stupa.
example.answer: Donations earned merit and recognition, so kings, guilds and ordinary men and women all contributed.

learn.reallife: Many Indian temples and gurdwaras today display donor plaques with names and towns, just as Sanchi's railings recorded donors 2,000 years ago.

topics.title: The structure of the stupa: Sanchi, Bharhut and Amaravati

learn.hook: From a simple mound of earth to a carved masterpiece with gateways bursting with stories: the stupa grew into one of India's greatest art forms.
points: The stupa (Sanskrit for 'heap') began as a simple semi-circular mound of earth, later called the anda. Gradually it became more complex, balancing round and square shapes.
Above the anda was the harmika, a balcony-like structure representing the abode of the gods. Arising from the harmika was a mast called the yashti, often surmounted by a chhatri or umbrella.
Around the mound was a railing, separating the sacred space from the secular world.
The early stupas at Sanchi and Bharhut were plain except for stone railings (resembling a bamboo or wooden fence) and gateways (toranas), richly carved and installed at the four cardinal points.
Later, the mound itself was elaborately carved with niches and sculptures, as at Amaravati (Andhra Pradesh) and Shah-ji-ki-Dheri in Peshawar (Pakistan).

example.q: Describe the parts of a stupa from the bottom up.
steps: Railing around the base, with gateways at four cardinal points.
Anda: the hemispherical mound.
Harmika: balcony-like structure on top, abode of the gods.
Yashti: mast rising from the harmika.
Chhatri: umbrella on the yashti.
example.answer: Railing and gateways → anda → harmika → yashti → chhatri.

learn.reallife: The Dhamek stupa at Sarnath and the Great Stupa at Sanchi are protected by the ASI and visited by thousands of tourists every year.

topics.title: 'Discovering' stupas: the fate of Amaravati and Sanchi

learn.hook: Some of Amaravati's finest carvings are in a museum in London, while Sanchi's stand where they were made. Why did one stupa survive and the other scatter?
points: In 1796 a local raja who wanted to build a temple stumbled upon the ruins of the stupa at Amaravati and decided to use its stone. Colin Mackenzie visited the site but did not publish his findings.

In 1854, Walter Elliot, the commissioner of Guntur (Andhra Pradesh), visited Amaravati and collected several sculpture panels which he took away to Madras (these came to be called the Elliot marbles). By the 1850s, some slabs had been taken to Calcutta, others to Madras and some to London. Many British administrators even used sculptures to decorate their gardens.

H.H. Cole, appointed Curator of Ancient Monuments in 1880, opposed the removal of antiquities, calling it a suicidal and indefensible policy to allow the country to be looted of original works of ancient art. He argued that museums should have plaster-cast facsimiles, while originals remained where they were found.

Cole could not save Amaravati, but in situ preservation was accepted for Sanchi. Sanchi survived partly because it escaped the eyes of railway contractors, builders and those looking for finds to carry to the museums of Europe.

Landmarks: 1814 founding of the Indian Museum, Calcutta; 1854 Cunningham's Bhilsa Topes, one of the earliest works on Sanchi; 1880 H.H. Cole appointed Curator of Ancient Monuments; 1914 Marshall and Foucher's The Monuments of Sanchi; 1989 Sanchi declared a World Heritage Site.

example.q: Why did Amaravati lose its sculptures while Sanchi kept them?
steps: Amaravati was discovered early, before scholars valued preserving monuments in place.
Its stones were reused and sculptures removed to Madras, Calcutta and London.
Sanchi escaped railway contractors and builders.
By then, ideas like Cole's about in situ preservation had gained ground.
example.answer: Amaravati was dismantled before in situ preservation was valued; Sanchi escaped notice longer and was preserved at the site.

learn.reallife: Debates continue today about returning Indian artefacts held abroad; India has recovered hundreds of antiquities from the USA, UK and Australia in recent years.

topics.title: Stories in stone and symbols of worship

learn.hook: In early Buddhist art, you will search in vain for the Buddha's face. Instead you find an empty seat, a wheel, a tree. Why?
points: Sculptures at stupas often tell stories. A scene on the northern gateway at Sanchi shows thatched huts and trees in a rural setting. Historians identified it as part of the Vessantara Jataka, the story of a generous prince who gave away everything to a Brahmana and went to live in the forest with his wife and children.
To understand such sculptures, historians compare them with textual evidence, such as Jatakas and other Buddhist texts. Without the texts, many sculptures would remain puzzling.
Many early sculptors did not show the Buddha in human form. Instead they showed his presence through symbols.

The empty seat was meant to indicate the meditation of the Buddha; the stupa represented the mahaparinibbana; the wheel stood for the first sermon at Sarnath; the tree symbolised an event in the Buddha's life (his enlightenment under a tree).
Such symbols are not to be read literally: a tree in this art is not just a tree, but stands for an event in the Buddha's life.

example.q: On a Sanchi panel you see a wheel above a seat with deer nearby. How would you interpret it?
steps: The wheel symbolises the first sermon.
The first sermon was given at Sarnath, at the deer park.
The seat suggests the Buddha's presence.
So the panel likely shows the first sermon at Sarnath.
example.answer: It probably represents the Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath, shown through symbols rather than a human figure.

learn.reallife: The dharma chakra (wheel) from Buddhist art is at the centre of India's national flag as the Ashoka Chakra.

quiz.explain: Texts help identify scenes.

They had not learnt to carve humans

quiz.explain: Early art suggested the Buddha's presence through symbols.

quiz.explain: Historians matched it with the Vessantara Jataka.

topics.title: Popular traditions in Buddhist art and debates on interpretation

learn.hook: A woman swinging from a tree on a Buddhist gateway? She is the shalabhanjika, whose touch was believed to make trees flower. She came from popular belief, not from Buddhist texts!
points: Some sculptures at Sanchi were not directly inspired by Buddhist ideas. A beautiful woman swinging from the edge of the gateway, holding a tree, was first thought to be merely decorative. Using non-Buddhist texts, scholars identified her as a shalabhanjika: in popular belief, a woman whose touch caused trees to flower and bear fruit. She was an auspicious symbol integrated into the stupa's decoration.
This shows that many people who turned to Buddhism enriched it with their own pre-Buddhist and even non-Buddhist beliefs, practices and ideas.
Animals such as elephants, horses, monkeys and cattle are carved at Sanchi. They were often used as symbols of human attributes; elephants, for example, signified strength and wisdom.

A woman surrounded by lotuses and elephants sprinkling water on her is identified by some historians as Maya, the Buddha's mother, and by others as Gajalakshmi, a popular goddess of good fortune associated with elephants. Devotees may have seen her as both. The serpent motif also appears on several pillars.

James Fergusson, an early art historian, considered Sanchi a centre of tree and serpent worship, because he was not familiar with Buddhist literature. His view shows how interpretations depend on what sources a scholar uses.

example.q: Why do historians disagree about the woman with elephants sprinkling water at Sanchi?
steps: Some read Buddhist texts and identify her as Maya, the Buddha's mother.
Others link her to popular traditions and identify her as Gajalakshmi.
Both readings fit the image.
Devotees themselves may have seen her in more than one way.
example.answer: The image fits both Buddhist and popular traditions, so she is identified as Maya by some and as Gajalakshmi by others.

learn.reallife: Gajalakshmi images are still painted on doorways and walls during Diwali in many Indian homes, showing the long life of this popular motif.

topics.title: New religious traditions: Mahayana Buddhism and Puranic Hinduism

learn.hook: Vishnu takes ten forms to save the world, while Bodhisattvas delay their own liberation to help others. Both ideas grew in the same centuries!
points: Around the beginning of the Common Era, Buddhist ideas changed. Earlier, achieving nibbana depended on personal effort, and the Buddha was regarded as a human who had attained enlightenment. Gradually the idea of a saviour emerged: the Buddha was seen as one who could ensure salvation.

Bodhisattvas were seen as deeply compassionate beings who accumulated merit through their efforts but used it not to attain nibbana and abandon the world, but to help others. Worship of images of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas became important. This new tradition was called Mahayana ('great vehicle'); followers of the older tradition, which Mahayana followers called Hinayana ('lesser vehicle'), described themselves as Theravadins, following the path of old, respected teachers, the theras.

Puranic Hinduism grew at the same time, with traditions like Vaishnavism, in which Vishnu was worshipped as the principal deity, and Shaivism, in which Shiva was regarded as the chief god. Worship was through bhakti, loving devotion to a chosen deity.

In Vaishnavism, cults developed around the avatars of Vishnu. Ten avatars were recognised: forms the deity assumed to save the world whenever it was threatened by disorder. Different avatars were popular in different regions, and local deities were often identified with them. Shiva was symbolised by the linga, and sometimes shown in human form. Images of deities carried attributes such as hairstyles, ornaments and objects held in their hands.

The Puranas contain stories about gods and goddesses, written in relatively simple Sanskrit verse, meant to be read aloud to everyone, including women and Shudras, who did not have access to Vedic learning. Much of their content evolved through interaction among people: priests, merchants and ordinary men and women.

example.q: How did Mahayana Buddhism differ from the older Theravada tradition?
steps: Theravada: nibbana through personal effort; the Buddha a human teacher.
Mahayana: the Buddha as saviour.
Mahayana: Bodhisattvas help others instead of entering nibbana.
Mahayana: worship of images of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas.
example.answer: Mahayana saw the Buddha as a saviour, honoured Bodhisattvas and worshipped images; Theravada stressed personal effort.

learn.reallife: Puranic stories reach every Indian child through Amar Chitra Katha comics, TV serials and grandparents' tales, much as the Puranas were meant to be read aloud to all.

topics.title: Building temples: from caves to Kailashnatha

learn.hook: At Ellora, sculptors carved an entire temple out of a single rock, from the top down. The chief sculptor reportedly exclaimed, 'Oh, how did I make it!'
points: Early temples were a small square room called the garbhagriha, with a single doorway for the worshipper to enter and offer worship to the image. Gradually a tall structure, the shikhara, was built over the central shrine. Temple walls were often decorated with sculpture.
Later temples became more elaborate, with assembly halls, huge walls and gateways, and arrangements for supplying water.

Some of the earliest temples were hollowed out of huge rocks as artificial caves. The tradition is very old: some of the earliest caves were made in the third century BCE on the orders of Asoka for renouncers of the Ajivika sect, in the Barabar hills (Bihar). Caves at Ajanta are famous for their paintings.

The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh (Uttar Pradesh), of about the fifth century CE, shows the developing temple form. The Kailashnatha temple at Ellora (Maharashtra), of the eighth century, was carved out of a single piece of rock.

Timeline of religious developments: Early Vedic traditions (c. 1500–1000 BCE) → later Vedic traditions (c. 1000–500 BCE) → early Upanishads, Jainism, Buddhism (c. sixth century BCE) → first stupas (c. third century BCE) → development of Mahayana, Vaishnavism, Shaivism and goddess cults → earliest temples.

example.q: How did the temple form develop over time?
steps: Start: a small square garbhagriha with one doorway.
Next: a tall shikhara built over the shrine.
Walls decorated with sculpture.
Later: assembly halls, walls, gateways, water supply.
example.answer: From a simple garbhagriha to temples with shikharas, sculpted walls, halls and gateways.

learn.reallife: The Kailasa (Kailashnatha) temple at Ellora is part of the Ellora Caves UNESCO World Heritage Site in Maharashtra, along with Buddhist and Jaina caves.

topics.title: Can we 'see' everything? Interpreting art and ritual

learn.hook: Is the giant relief at Mamallapuram the Ganga descending from heaven, or Arjuna doing penance? Scholars still argue, and both sides have good reasons!
points: When nineteenth-century European scholars first saw sculptures of gods and goddesses, they did not understand them. Images with multiple arms and heads, or combining human and animal forms, seemed grotesque to them.

They tried to make sense of these by comparing them with ancient Greek art, which they knew. Early images of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas from Gandhara (Taxila and Peshawar) closely resembled Greek models, so these scholars considered them the best examples of early Indian art. This was a strategy of understanding the unfamiliar through the familiar, but it judged Indian art by foreign standards.

Sometimes texts and images do not match neatly. The huge relief at Mamallapuram (Tamil Nadu) is identified by some as the Descent of the Ganga from heaven, using the natural cleft through the middle of the rock. Others think it shows Arjuna doing penance on the river bank to obtain weapons, pointing to the central ascetic figure.

Many rituals, religious beliefs and practices did not leave permanent traces in the form of monuments, sculpture or paintings. These include everyday practices and those associated with special occasions. Historians therefore cannot 'see' everything and must be aware of the limits of their evidence.

example.q: Why is it problematic to judge Indian sculpture by Greek standards?
steps: Greek art had its own ideals of the human body.
Indian sculpture expressed different ideas, like multiple arms showing divine power.
Judging by Greek standards made Indian images look 'grotesque' and Gandhara images look 'best'.
So it ignored the meanings within Indian traditions.
example.answer: Because it measures Indian art against a foreign ideal and misses the meanings it carried in its own tradition.

learn.reallife: The Mamallapuram monuments are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Tamil Nadu holds a dance festival there each year with the carved rocks as a backdrop.

chapters.title: Part II: Through the Eyes of Travellers: Perceptions of Society

topics.title: Travellers' accounts as sources

learn.hook: Imagine describing a mango to someone who has never seen one. Medieval travellers had to do exactly that for readers back home, and in doing so they left us priceless records!
points: Historians use accounts by travellers who visited the subcontinent between the tenth and seventeenth centuries to learn about social life. Many came from very different social and cultural backgrounds.
People travelled for many reasons: in search of work, to escape natural disasters, as traders, merchants, soldiers, priests and pilgrims, or simply driven by a sense of adventure.
Outsiders often noticed things that locals took for granted and did not record, which makes their accounts valuable.

But their perspectives had limits: they often compared what they saw with their own societies, could misunderstand unfamiliar practices, depended on their informants, and sometimes generalised from a few cases.

Major travellers: Al-Biruni (973–1048, from Uzbekistan), Marco Polo (1254–1323, Italy), Ibn Battuta (1304–77, Morocco), Abdur Razzaq Samarqandi (1413–82, Samarqand), Afanasii Nikitin (in India 1466–72, Russia), Duarte Barbosa (Portugal; visited 1518), Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (1605–89, France) and Francois Bernier (1620–88, France).

example.q: A traveller writes that 'all Indians eat with their right hand only'. What should a historian ask before using this?
steps: Where and among whom did he observe this?
Was he generalising from a few people?
Was he comparing with his own society?
Can other sources confirm it?
example.answer: She should check the traveller's context, informants and possible generalisation, and compare with other sources.

learn.reallife: Today's travel vloggers and foreign correspondents writing about India are a modern version of these travellers: insightful, but also shaped by what they find unusual.

topics.title: Al-Biruni and the Kitab-ul-Hind

learn.hook: Taken to Ghazni as a hostage, Al-Biruni ended up learning Sanskrit and writing one of the most detailed books on India ever produced by an outsider!
points: Al-Biruni was born in 973 in Khwarizm, in present-day Uzbekistan. He was an expert in several languages: Syriac, Arabic, Persian, Hebrew and Sanskrit. He did not know Greek but knew the works of Plato and other Greek philosophers through Arabic translations.

In 1017, when Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni invaded Khwarizm, he took several scholars and poets back to his capital, Ghazni; Al-Biruni was one of them. He arrived as a hostage but grew to like the city and spent the rest of his life there.
When the Punjab became part of the Ghaznavid empire, he spent years in the company of Brahmana priests and scholars, learnt Sanskrit, and studied religious and philosophical texts.

His Kitab-ul-Hind, written in Arabic in a simple and lucid style, has 80 chapters on subjects such as religion and philosophy, festivals, astronomy, alchemy, manners and customs, social life, weights and measures, iconography, laws and metrology.

Each chapter has a distinctive structure: it begins with a question, follows with a description based on Sanskritic traditions, and concludes with a comparison with other cultures. This geometric structure, notable for precision and predictability, reflects his mathematical bent. He probably wrote for people living along the frontiers of the subcontinent.

example.q: Describe the structure of a Kitab-ul-Hind chapter.
steps: Step 1: Open with a question.
Step 2: Describe the subject using Sanskritic traditions.
Step 3: Compare it with other cultures.
example.answer: Question → description from Sanskritic traditions → comparison with other cultures.

learn.reallife: Uzbekistan and India have honoured Al-Biruni as a symbol of shared scholarship; his work on Indian astronomy is still cited by historians of science.

topics.title: Ibn Battuta's Rihla: a globetrotter from Tangier

learn.hook: Ibn Battuta travelled about as far as anyone of his age: Morocco, Mecca, Delhi, the Maldives, China. And he dictated it all to a scribe once he got home!
points: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier (Morocco) in 1304 into a respectable and educated family known for expertise in Islamic religious law (sharia). He received a literary and scholastic education.
Before reaching India, he had made pilgrimages to Mecca and travelled extensively in Syria, Iraq, Persia, Yemen, Oman and a few trading ports on the coast of East Africa.

Travelling overland through Central Asia, he reached Sind in 1333. Hearing of Muhammad bin Tughlaq's generosity as a patron of arts and letters, he set off for Delhi via Multan and Uch. The Sultan was impressed by his scholarship and appointed him qazi (judge) of Delhi. He later fell out of favour and was imprisoned, then restored to service.

In 1342 he was ordered to proceed to China as the Sultan's envoy to the Mongol ruler. He went to the Malabar coast through central India, then to the Maldives (where he was qazi for eighteen months), Sri Lanka, back to Malabar, then Bengal and Assam, took a ship to Sumatra and another to the Chinese port of Zaitun. He returned home in 1347.

His travel account, the Rihla, written in Arabic, was recorded by Ibn Juzayy, who was deputed by the ruler of Morocco to write down what Ibn Battuta dictated. It gives rich details of social and cultural life in the subcontinent in the fourteenth century.

example.q: Trace Ibn Battuta's journey from Delhi as the Sultan's envoy to China.
steps: Delhi → Malabar coast via central India.
Malabar → Maldives → Sri Lanka.
Back to Malabar and Maldives → Bengal and Assam.

topics.title: Curiosities, coconuts and the dangers of the road

learn.hook: How would you describe a coconut to someone in Morocco? Ibn Battuta said it looked exactly like a man's head!
points: Ibn Battuta considered experience gained through travel a more important source of knowledge than books. He loved travelling and was always eager for new experiences; he especially valued curiosities.

Travel was hard and dangerous. He was attacked by bands of robbers several times. Although he preferred travelling in caravans with companions, this did not deter highway robbers: on the way from Multan to Delhi his caravan was attacked, many travellers lost their lives, and the survivors, including him, were severely wounded.
Travellers also suffered from homesickness and illness on long journeys.

To describe unfamiliar things, Ibn Battuta compared them with what his readers knew. He wrote that the coconut 'resembles a man's head', with what look like two eyes and a mouth, the inside like a brain when green, and fibres like hair.
He described paan (betel) as a plant grown like grapevines, cultivated only for its leaves, which people ate after chewing areca nut.

example.q: Why did Ibn Battuta compare the coconut to a man's head?
steps: His readers in North Africa had never seen a coconut.
He needed a familiar image to explain its shape and parts.
Eyes, mouth, brain and hair are things everyone knows.
So the comparison made the unfamiliar easy to picture.
example.answer: To help readers who had never seen a coconut imagine it, using a familiar comparison.

learn.reallife: Kerala's name is often linked to 'kera', the coconut palm; coconuts and paan are still everyday sights there, just as Ibn Battuta found on the Malabar coast.

topics.title: Francois Bernier: a doctor with a difference

learn.hook: A French doctor at the Mughal court wrote letters home that shaped how Europe thought of India for two centuries. Was he fair?
points: Francois Bernier, a Frenchman, was a doctor, political philosopher and historian. Like many others, he came to the Mughal empire in search of opportunities. He was in India for twelve years, from 1656 to 1668.

He was closely associated with the Mughal court, first as physician to Prince Dara Shukoh, the eldest son of Emperor Shah Jahan, and later as an intellectual and scientist with Danishmand Khan, an Armenian noble at the Mughal court.
He travelled to several parts of the country and wrote accounts of what he saw. He compared what he saw in India with the situation in Europe, generally emphasising the superiority of Europe.
His major work, Travels in the Mogul Empire, was dedicated to the French king Louis XIV. Many of his other works were written as letters to influential officials and ministers.

Other European travellers include Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (a French jeweller who travelled to India at least six times and was fascinated by trading conditions), Manucci (an Italian doctor who never returned to Europe and settled in India) and Duarte Barbosa (a Portuguese writer who described trade and society in south India).

example.q: Why did Bernier write his works mainly for European rulers and officials, and how might this affect his account?
steps: He dedicated his main work to Louis XIV and wrote letters to ministers.
He wanted to influence policy-makers in Europe.
He therefore used India as a contrast to argue for European ideas.
So his account may exaggerate India's 'faults' to make his point.
example.answer: Writing for European decision-makers, he used India as a contrast to support his views, which can make his account one-sided.

learn.reallife: Many Indian doctors work abroad today in the UK and USA, just as Bernier, a European doctor, once served at the Mughal court.

topics.title: Al-Biruni and the Sanskritic tradition: making sense of caste

learn.hook: Al-Biruni accepted much of what the Brahmanical texts said about caste, but he rejected one idea completely: that people could be permanently 'polluted'.
points: Al-Biruni discussed several barriers to understanding India. The first was language: Sanskrit was so different from Arabic and Persian that ideas and concepts could not easily be translated. The second was the difference in religious beliefs and practices. The third was the self-absorption and consequent insularity of the local population.

Despite these barriers, he relied almost exclusively on the works of Brahmanas, often citing the Vedas, the Puranas, the Bhagavad Gita, the works of Patanjali and the Manusmriti. So his picture of society was shaped by normative Sanskrit texts.

He tried to explain the caste system by looking for parallels in other societies. He noted that ancient Persia recognised four social categories: knights and princes; monks, fire-priests and lawyers; physicians, astronomers and other scientists; and peasants and artisans. So social divisions were not unique to India. He also noted that within Islam all men were considered equal, differing only in their observance of piety.

He accepted the Brahmanical description of caste but disapproved of the notion of pollution. He argued that everything which falls into impurity strives to regain its original purity: the sun cleanses the air and salt in the sea keeps water from becoming polluted. Without this, life on earth would be impossible. So social pollution was contrary to the laws of nature.

He described the antyaja ('born outside the system'), who were not included in the caste order and were often expected to provide inexpensive labour to peasants and zamindars. Historians note that the reality of caste was not as rigid as the normative texts he used suggest.

example.q: Explain Al-Biruni's argument against the idea of pollution.
steps: He observed that nature constantly restores purity.
The sun cleanses the air; salt keeps the sea from becoming polluted.
If impurity were permanent, life on earth would be impossible.
So the idea of permanent social pollution goes against the laws of nature.
example.answer: He argued that, as everything in nature regains purity, a permanent social pollution is contrary to nature's laws.

learn.reallife: Article 17 of the Indian Constitution abolished untouchability and made its practice in any form an offence, rejecting the idea of social pollution.

topics.title: Ibn Battuta on cities, bazaars, crops and textiles

learn.hook: Ibn Battuta found Delhi the largest city in India, with walls eleven cubits thick and 28 gates. Daulatabad, he said, was just as grand!
points: Ibn Battuta found cities in the subcontinent full of exciting opportunities for those who had the necessary drive, resources and skills. They were densely populated and prosperous, except when disrupted by wars and invasions.

He described Delhi as a vast city with a great population, the largest in India. Its rampart was without parallel, with walls eleven cubits thick, houses for night sentries and gatekeepers, storehouses for grain and weapons, and 28 gates (the Budaun darwaza being the greatest). Daulatabad (in Maharashtra) was no less in size and easily rivalled Delhi.

Bazaars were not only places of economic exchange but also hubs of social and cultural activities. In Daulatabad there was a market for male and female singers, known as Tarababad, one of the greatest and most beautiful bazaars, with many shops, carpets, a huge dome and mosques for prayer.
Agriculture was very productive because of the fertility of the soil, which allowed peasants to cultivate two crops a year.

The subcontinent was well integrated with inter-Asian trade networks. Indian textiles, especially cotton cloth, fine muslins, silks, brocade and satin, were in great demand in West and Southeast Asia, fetching huge profits. Certain fine muslins were so expensive that only the very wealthy could wear them.

example.q: What does Ibn Battuta's account suggest about the economy of fourteenth-century India?
steps: Fertile soil allowed two crops a year.
Big cities like Delhi and Daulatabad were prosperous.
Bazaars were busy centres of trade and culture.
Indian textiles earned huge profits abroad.
example.answer: It suggests a prosperous economy with productive agriculture, thriving cities and strong export trade in textiles.

learn.reallife: India is still among the world's largest exporters of cotton textiles and yarn, continuing a trade that made Indian cloth famous across Asia in Ibn Battuta's time.

topics.title: A unique system of communication

learn.hook: News from Sind could reach the Sultan in Delhi in just five days, while merchants needed fifty. How? Relay runners with bells!
points: The state took special measures to encourage merchants. Almost all trade routes were well supplied with inns and guest houses.
Ibn Battuta was amazed by the efficiency of the postal system, which allowed merchants not only to send information and remit credit across long distances, but also to dispatch goods at short notice.
There were two kinds of postal system. The horse-post, called uluq, was run by royal horses stationed at a distance of every four miles.

The foot-post, called dawa, had three stations per mile. At every third of a mile there was a well-populated village, outside which were three pavilions. Men sat ready; one would run with the letter in one hand and a rod with bells in the other, and the next runner, hearing the bells, would be ready to take over. The foot-post was quicker than the horse-post.

It was sometimes used to transport fruits from Khurasan that were much liked in India. A journey from Sind to Delhi took fifty days, but news reports of spies reached the Sultan in just five days through the postal system.

example.q: How many times faster was the postal system than an ordinary journey from Sind to Delhi?
steps: Ordinary journey: 50 days.
Postal system: 5 days.
example.answer: About 10 times faster.

learn.reallife: India Post, with over 1.5 lakh post offices, the largest postal network in the world, carries on a tradition of relays that goes back to the dawa and uluq.

topics.title: Bernier and the 'degenerate' East: the question of landownership

learn.hook: One mistaken idea, that the Mughal emperor owned all the land, travelled from Bernier to Montesquieu to Marx, and shaped European theories about Asia for centuries.
points: Bernier's account works on a binary model: India is presented as the inverse of Europe. Europe stands for progress and rationality; India for backwardness.

He believed one fundamental difference was the lack of private property in land in Mughal India. He thought the emperor owned all the land and distributed it among nobles. A firm believer in private property, he saw crown ownership as harmful for both the state and its people.

In his view, because landholders could not pass on their land to their children, they avoided long-term investment in production. This led to the uniform ruin of agriculture, excessive oppression of the peasantry and a continuous decline in living standards, except for the ruling aristocracy. He saw Indian society as a mass of impoverished people dominated by a small, very rich ruling class, with no middle class; he warned that European kingdoms following this model would be ruined.

His ideas influenced Montesquieu, who developed the theory of oriental despotism (Asian rulers enjoying absolute authority over subjects kept in poverty), and later Karl Marx, who developed the idea of the Asiatic mode of production, in which the state appropriated surplus from self-sufficient village communities.

But Mughal official documents do not suggest that the state was the sole owner of land. Abu'l Fazl described land revenue as a 'remuneration of sovereignty', a claim made by the ruler for protection, not rent on land he owned. European travellers may have mistaken it for rent because the revenue demand was often very high. In contrast, Ibn Battuta, writing three centuries earlier, described prosperity and opportunity, showing how differently travellers could see India.

example.q: Compare Ibn Battuta's and Bernier's views of India.
steps: Ibn Battuta: excited by the unfamiliar; describes prosperous cities, bazaars, two crops, valued textiles.
Bernier: compares India with Europe; stresses decline, oppression and lack of private property.
Ibn Battuta had no political agenda of comparison; Bernier wrote to influence European rulers.
So their purposes shaped their pictures.
example.answer: Ibn Battuta saw prosperity and novelty; Bernier saw decline in contrast to Europe, largely because of their different purposes and frames.

learn.reallife: Debates on land rights continue in India today, from tenancy reforms in West Bengal (Operation Barga) to land records digitisation under the Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme.

topics.title: A more complex social reality: towns and merchants

learn.hook: Bernier called Mughal cities 'camp towns' that would die if the emperor left. Yet about 15 per cent of people lived in towns, more than in western Europe then!
points: Bernier's own account reveals a more complex reality. He noted that artisans had no incentive to improve quality because profits were taken by the state, so manufacturing was declining. Yet he also admitted that vast quantities of the world's precious metals flowed into India because Indian manufactures were exported in exchange for gold and silver. He also noticed a prosperous merchant community engaged in long-distance trade.
In the seventeenth century about 15 per cent of the population lived in towns, on average a higher proportion than in western Europe at the time.

Still, Bernier described Mughal cities as 'camp towns': towns that owed their existence, and depended for survival, on the imperial camp. He believed they came into existence when the court moved in and rapidly declined when it moved out.
In reality there were many kinds of towns: manufacturing towns, trading towns, port towns, sacred centres and pilgrimage towns.

Merchants often had strong community or kin ties and were organised into caste-cum-occupational bodies. In western India these groups were called mahajans and their chief a sheth. In cities like Ahmedabad, the mahajans were collectively represented by the chief of the merchant community, the nagarsheth. Other urban groups included physicians (hakim or vaid), teachers (pundit or mulla), lawyers (wakil), painters, architects, musicians and calligraphers.

example.q: What does Bernier's own description of urban centres reveal that contradicts his 'camp town' idea?
steps: He admits precious metals flowed into India for its manufactures.
He notes a prosperous merchant community.
About 15% of people lived in towns.
Many towns were manufacturing, trading, port or pilgrimage centres, not dependent on the court.
example.answer: It reveals a thriving urban economy with merchants and diverse towns, which does not fit the idea that towns depended only on the imperial camp.

learn.reallife: Ahmedabad's tradition of merchant organisation continues in today's mahajans, chambers of commerce and the city's status as a UNESCO World Heritage City (2017).

topics.title: Women: slaves, sati and labourers

learn.hook: Travellers wrote about women as slaves, as widows on funeral pyres, and as workers in fields and markets. Each account shows only part of the picture.
points: Ibn Battuta wrote that slaves were openly sold in markets like any other commodity and were regularly exchanged as gifts. On reaching Sind he bought 'horses, camels and slaves' as gifts for Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq; in Multan he presented the governor with a slave and a horse along with raisins and almonds.

There was considerable differentiation among slaves. Some female slaves in the Sultan's service were experts in music and dance; the Sultan also employed female slaves to keep a watch on his nobles. Slaves were generally used for domestic labour, including carrying people in palanquins (dola). The price of slaves, especially female slaves for domestic work, was very low, and most families who could afford it kept at least one or two.

Bernier chose the practice of sati for detailed description. He noted that while some women seemed to embrace death cheerfully, others were forced. He described the sati of a child widow of about twelve at Lahore, forced to the pyre, as a cruel practice.

Women's lives involved much more than sati. Their labour was crucial in both agricultural and non-agricultural production. Women from merchant families took part in commercial activities, sometimes even taking mercantile disputes to court.
Travellers noticed the seclusion of some elite women, but women's wide participation in work and trade makes it unlikely that women in general were confined to the private spaces of their homes.

example.q: What does Ibn Battuta's account reveal about slavery in the Delhi Sultanate?
steps: Slaves were sold openly in markets and given as gifts.
Slaves were differentiated: some were skilled musicians or used as spies.
Most were used for domestic labour and palanquin-carrying.
Prices were low, so many families kept slaves.
example.answer: Slavery was widespread and varied: slaves were traded and gifted, used for many tasks, and cheap enough for many households.

learn.reallife: Sati was banned in British India in 1829, and the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987 makes even glorifying it an offence in India today.

chapters.title: Part II: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts

topics.title: A mosaic of beliefs: the integration of cults

learn.hook: At Puri, a wooden image carved by local tribal specialists came to be worshipped as Jagannatha, a form of Vishnu. How do local gods join a larger tradition?
points: From about the eighth century, sculpture and texts show a striking variety of gods and goddesses, such as Vishnu, Shiva and many forms of the goddess, worshipped across the subcontinent.

Historians see at least two processes at work. One was the spread of Brahmanical ideas through the composition, compilation and preservation of Puranic texts in simple Sanskrit verse, accessible to women and Shudras. The other was that Brahmanas accepted and reworked the beliefs and practices of other social groups.

At Puri (Odisha), by the twelfth century, a local deity, whose image was and still is made of wood by local tribal specialists, came to be identified as a form of Vishnu: Jagannatha, literally 'lord of the world'.

Local goddesses, often worshipped as a stone smeared with ochre, were incorporated into the Puranic framework by being identified as wives of the principal male deities: sometimes Lakshmi, wife of Vishnu, and sometimes Parvati, wife of Shiva.

The sociologist Robert Redfield described the practices of dominant groups such as priests and rulers as the 'great' tradition and those of peasants and others as 'little' traditions. He noted that both changed through their interaction.

example.q: How do historians explain the integration of a local deity like Jagannatha into a wider tradition?
steps: A local deity had its own worshippers and tribal specialists.
Brahmanas identified it with Vishnu, a Puranic god.
Its worship then became part of a wider Vaishnava tradition, while keeping local features.
This illustrates interaction between 'great' and 'little' traditions.
example.answer: By showing how a local deity was identified with a Puranic god, which blended local and Brahmanical traditions.

learn.reallife: The annual Rath Yatra of Lord Jagannatha at Puri draws lakhs of devotees, and the wooden images are still renewed in the Nabakalebara ceremony.

topics.title: Tantra, conflict and two kinds of bhakti

learn.hook: Some worshipped a god with a face, ornaments and stories; others worshipped a god beyond all form. Both paths are called bhakti!
points: Tantric practices were widespread in several parts of the subcontinent. They were open to women and men, and practitioners often ignored differences of caste and class within the ritual context.
Many Tantric ideas influenced Shaivism and Buddhism, especially in the eastern, northern and southern parts of the subcontinent. Tantric practitioners often ignored the authority of the Vedas.

There were often tensions: those who valued the Vedic tradition condemned practices outside regulated sacrifice; devotees often projected their chosen deity, Vishnu or Shiva, as supreme. Relations with Buddhism and Jainism were also often tense, if not marked by open conflict.

Bhakti traditions are classified into two broad categories. Saguna bhakti ('with attributes') focuses on specific deities such as Shiva, Vishnu and his avatars, and forms of the goddess, often in human form. Nirguna bhakti ('without attributes') is the worship of an abstract form of god.

Timeline of religious teachers: Appar and Sambandar (Tamil Nadu, c. 6th–8th centuries) → Andal and Nammalvar (Tamil Nadu, c. 8th–9th) → Basavanna (Karnataka, 12th) → Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi, 14th) → Kabir, Guru Nanak (15th–16th) → Mirabai (16th).

example.q: Classify: (a) worship of Krishna as a beloved with a flute; (b) devotion to a formless Ultimate Reality.
steps: Krishna has a form, stories and attributes.
So (a) is saguna bhakti.
A formless reality has no attributes.
So (b) is nirguna bhakti.
example.answer: (a) saguna; (b) nirguna.

learn.reallife: Bhajans to Krishna sung at ISKCON temples (saguna) and the Gurbani hymns sung in gurdwaras to the formless Waheguru (nirguna) show both bhakti forms alive today.
