topics.title: An auction in Burdwan and the Permanent Settlement

learn.hook: In 1797, estates of the Raja of Burdwan were auctioned for unpaid revenue. Many 'buyers' turned out to be the Raja's own agents!
points: In 1797 an auction was held in Burdwan (present-day Bardhaman). Several mahals (estates) held by the Raja of Burdwan were sold because he had accumulated huge arrears of revenue.

Many of the purchasers were the Raja's own servants and agents who bought the lands on his behalf. These were benami purchases (literally 'anonymous'), made in the name of an insignificant person while the real beneficiary stayed hidden. In this way the Raja kept control of his estates.

The auctions were a result of the Permanent Settlement introduced in Bengal in 1793 by the East India Company under Governor-General Lord Cornwallis. The revenue each zamindar had to pay was fixed permanently, and estates of those who failed to pay were auctioned.

The Company saw rajas and taluqdars as zamindars. A zamindar was not a landowner in the village but a revenue collector of the state; a zamindari could include as many as 400 villages. Zamindars collected rent from ryots and paid fixed revenue to the Company.

Aims: Bengal's economy was in crisis, with recurrent famines and falling output. Officials hoped that fixing revenue permanently would ensure a regular flow of revenue to the Company, encourage investment in land (since landholders would keep any increased profits), and create a class of loyal landholders and 'improving' farmers with capital and enterprise.

example.q: How did the Raja of Burdwan keep control of his estates despite the auction?
steps: His estates were auctioned for arrears.
His own agents bought many of them.
These were benami purchases in other people's names.
So the Raja remained the real controller.
example.answer: Through benami purchases by his agents, so the estates stayed under his control.

learn.reallife: The Permanent Settlement was finally ended after independence when West Bengal passed the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, abolishing zamindari.

topics.title: Why zamindars defaulted

learn.hook: If the revenue did not reach the treasury by sunset on the due date, the zamindari could be auctioned. That was the 'Sunset Law'!
points: Revenue arrears were common, and many zamindaris were auctioned in the decades after the Permanent Settlement. Several reasons explain this.

First, the initial demand was very high. Since the demand was fixed for all time, the Company feared it could never claim a share of increased income later, so it pegged the demand high, arguing the burden would fall as production expanded and prices rose.

Second, this high demand was imposed in the 1790s, when prices of agricultural produce were depressed, making it hard for ryots to pay their dues to the zamindar. Third, the revenue was invariable, regardless of the harvest, and had to be paid punctually; under the Sunset Law, if payment did not come in by sunset of the specified date, the zamindari could be auctioned.

Fourth, the Settlement initially limited the zamindar's power to collect rent and manage the zamindari. Zamindars' troops were disbanded, customs duties abolished, and their cutcheries (courts) brought under the supervision of a Collector appointed by the Company. They lost the power to organise local justice and police; the collectorate became an alternative centre of authority.
Fifth, ryots sometimes delayed payment deliberately, encouraged by rich peasants, and harvests were uneven. Zamindars could take defaulting ryots to court, but justice was slow.

example.q: Why were so many zamindaris auctioned after the Permanent Settlement?
steps: Revenue demand was set very high.
Agricultural prices were low in the 1790s.
The Sunset Law required punctual payment regardless of harvest.
Zamindars' powers over troops and courts were curtailed.
Ryots delayed payment, and courts were slow.
example.answer: Because of high fixed demand, low prices, the rigid Sunset Law, reduced zamindari powers and ryots' resistance.

learn.reallife: Modern loans also have strict due dates and penalties; the Sunset Law was an extreme version where one missed sunset could cost an entire estate.

topics.title: The rise of the jotedars

learn.hook: While zamindars struggled, a group of rich peasants in the villages of north Bengal grew so powerful that they could defy zamindars and even buy their estates!
points: By the end of the eighteenth century, rich peasants were consolidating their position in villages. In parts of Bengal they were called jotedars; elsewhere haoladars, gantidars or mandals. Francis Buchanan's survey of Dinajpur district vividly describes the jotedars.

By the early nineteenth century, jotedars had acquired vast areas of land, sometimes several thousand acres. They controlled local trade and moneylending, exercising immense power over poorer cultivators.
Much of their land was cultivated by sharecroppers (adhiyars or bargadars), who brought their own ploughs, worked the fields and handed over half the produce to the jotedar after the harvest.

Unlike zamindars, who often lived in towns, jotedars lived in the villages, so their power within villages was more effective. They fiercely resisted zamindars' efforts to increase the jama (revenue) of the village, prevented zamindari officials from doing their work, mobilised dependent ryots and deliberately delayed revenue payments.
When zamindars' estates were auctioned for arrears, jotedars were often among the purchasers. They were most powerful in north Bengal.

example.answer: Because of their land, control of trade and credit, residence in villages, and the dependence of poorer cultivators.

topics.title: Zamindars resist, and the Fifth Report

learn.hook: Over 800 of the Fifth Report's 1,002 pages were appendices: petitions, collectors' reports and tables. It was a monster of a document, and it had an agenda!
points: Zamindars found ways to survive. The Raja of Burdwan first transferred part of his zamindari to his mother, since the Company had decreed that the property of women would not be taken over.

At auctions, zamindars' agents manipulated the proceedings: they outbid genuine buyers and then refused to pay, so the estate had to be resold; this was repeated until the price fell and the zamindar's agent bought it cheaply. Through such fictitious sales and benami purchases, zamindars kept control. Lathyals (lathi-wielding strongmen) sometimes drove off outside buyers, and ryots also resisted outsiders.
By the early nineteenth century the depression in prices ended. Zamindars who had survived the 1790s consolidated their power, and the Company relaxed its rules of revenue payment.

The Fifth Report, submitted to the British Parliament in 1813, was the fifth of a series of reports on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India. It ran to 1,002 pages, of which over 800 were appendices reproducing petitions of zamindars and ryots, reports of collectors, statistical tables and notes on revenue and judicial administration of Bengal and Madras.

In Britain, many groups attacked the Company's monopoly and its officials' corruption, and Parliament passed Acts to regulate Company rule and demanded regular reports. The Fifth Report became the basis of intense debates. Historians note it exaggerated the collapse of traditional zamindari power and the scale on which zamindars were losing land.

example.answer: Through transfers to women, fictitious sales, benami purchases and force against outsiders.

topics.title: The hoe: Buchanan and the Paharias

learn.hook: Plains zamindars paid tribute to hill chiefs to stop raids, and traders paid tolls to use mountain passes. The Paharias were masters of their hills!
points: Francis Buchanan was a physician in the Bengal Medical Service who undertook detailed surveys for the East India Company. In 1810–11 he travelled through the Rajmahal hills. He looked at the landscape as a Company employee, judging its potential for 'improvement' and commercial value.

The Paharias lived around the Rajmahal hills. They subsisted on forest produce and practised shifting cultivation: they cleared patches by cutting bushes and burning undergrowth, which enriched the soil with potash, and grew pulses and millets, scratching the ground lightly with hoes. After a few years they left the land fallow.

They collected mahua flowers for food, silk cocoons and resin for sale, and wood for charcoal. Their identity was intimately linked with the forest. Their chiefs maintained unity, settled disputes and led the tribe in battles.

The Paharias regularly raided the plains where settled farmers lived. Raids helped them survive in years of scarcity, asserted their power over settled communities, and were a way of negotiating political relations with outsiders.

Plains zamindars purchased peace by paying regular tribute to hill chiefs. Traders paid a small amount for permission to use passes controlled by them; once paid, Paharia chiefs protected the traders' goods.

example.q: How did the Paharias respond to outsiders before the late eighteenth century?
steps: They raided the plains, especially in years of scarcity.
Zamindars paid them tribute for peace.
Traders paid them to use hill passes, and were protected in return.
So they negotiated power with outsiders on their own terms.
example.answer: Through raids and negotiated arrangements: tribute from zamindars and payments from traders in return for peace and protection.

learn.reallife: Mahua flowers are still collected by tribal communities in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh, and are an important minor forest produce today.

topics.title: The plough: pacification, Santhals and Damin-i-Koh

learn.hook: From 40 Santhal villages in 1838 to 1,473 by 1851: the Damin-i-Koh filled with plough farmers, and the Paharias were pushed deeper into the hills.
points: In the last decades of the eighteenth century, settled agriculture expanded aggressively in eastern India. To the British, extending settled agriculture would enlarge land revenue, produce crops for export and create a settled, ordered society. They saw forest people as savage, unruly and difficult to govern.

In the 1770s the British followed a brutal policy of extermination, hunting down and killing Paharias. By the 1780s, Augustus Cleveland, the Collector of Bhagalpur, proposed pacification: Paharia chiefs were given an annual allowance and made responsible for their men's conduct. Many refused; those who accepted lost authority in their community as stipendaries of the government. Many Paharias withdrew deep into the mountains.

Around 1800 the Santhals began coming into the area. They cleared forests, cut timber, ploughed the land and grew rice and cotton. The British saw them as ideal settlers: hardworking and good at reclaiming land. Zamindars also hired them to expand cultivation.

In 1832 a large area was demarcated as the Damin-i-Koh, declared the land of the Santhals. They were to live within it and practise plough agriculture. The land grant required that at least one-tenth of the area be cleared and cultivated within the first ten years. The area was surveyed, mapped and enclosed by boundary pillars.

Santhal settlements grew rapidly: from 40 villages in 1838 to 1,473 villages by 1851, and the population rose from about 3,000 to over 82,000. As Santhals occupied the lower hills, the Paharias had to recede further. This was a conflict between the hoe, symbol of shifting cultivation, and the plough, symbol of settled agriculture.

example.q: Why is the story of the Rajmahal hills called a conflict between the hoe and the plough?
steps: Paharias used the hoe for shifting cultivation.
Santhals used the plough for settled farming.
The British favoured the plough and gave land to Santhals.
As Santhals expanded, Paharias lost land and moved deeper into the hills.
example.answer: Because the plough-using Santhals, backed by the British, expanded at the expense of the hoe-using Paharias.

learn.reallife: The Santhal Pargana division of Jharkhand, with towns like Dumka and Sahibganj, grew out of the Damin-i-Koh area.

topics.title: The Santhal rebellion and Buchanan's account as a source

learn.hook: The Santhals cleared forests to farm, but soon found their land slipping away to taxes, moneylenders and zamindars. In 1855 they rose in revolt, the hul!
points: The Santhals soon found that the land they had brought under cultivation was slipping away. The state levied heavy taxes; moneylenders (dikus) charged high rates of interest and took over land when debts were unpaid; and zamindars asserted control over the Damin area.

By the 1850s the Santhals felt the time had come to rebel against zamindars, moneylenders and the colonial state, to create an ideal world where they would rule themselves. The Santhal rebellion (hul) of 1855–56 was led by figures such as Sidhu and Kanhu.

After the revolt, the Santhal Pargana was created, carved out of the districts of Bhagalpur and Birbhum (about 5,500 square miles). The colonial state hoped that a new territory with some special laws would conciliate the Santhals.
Buchanan's account is a valuable source: it describes landscapes, crops, settlements, forest products and peoples in rich detail.

But it also has limits. Buchanan wrote as a Company employee, interested in resources and 'improvement'; he was critical of forest dwellers' ways of life and saw forests as land to be turned into fields. His account reveals what the Company valued, and conceals how local people themselves saw their world.

example.q: Why did the Santhals rebel against British rule?
steps: Heavy taxes were imposed on their land.
Moneylenders charged high interest and took over land.
Zamindars asserted control over the Damin area.
The colonial state backed this system, so they rose against all three.
example.answer: Because taxes, moneylenders and zamindars, backed by the colonial state, were taking away their land and freedom.

learn.reallife: Hul Diwas is observed every year on 30 June in Jharkhand to remember the Santhal rebellion and its leaders.

topics.title: Account books come to be burnt: Supa, 1875

learn.hook: On 12 May 1875, ryots in Supa village near Poona demanded the moneylenders' account books and set them on fire. Paper had become a symbol of oppression!
points: On 12 May 1875, ryots from surrounding rural areas gathered at Supa, a large village in Poona district (present-day Maharashtra), where many shopkeepers and moneylenders lived.

They attacked the shopkeepers and moneylenders (sahukars), demanding their bahi khatas (account books) and debt bonds. They burnt the khatas, looted grain shops and in some cases set fire to sahukars' houses.

From Poona the revolt spread to Ahmednagar, and over the next two months to many more villages. Everywhere the pattern was similar: sahukars were attacked, account books burnt and debt bonds destroyed.
Terrified sahukars fled their villages, often leaving their property behind. British police posts were set up in villages, and many people were arrested and convicted.
The ryots' anger focused on the account books and bonds because these records were the instruments through which they believed they had been cheated and trapped in debt.

example.q: Why did the ryots target account books and debt bonds rather than just the moneylenders?
steps: The books and bonds recorded their debts.
They believed the entries were manipulated.
Destroying them wiped out the proof of debt.
So the documents themselves were seen as instruments of oppression.
example.answer: Because the books and bonds were the legal proof of debts they felt were unjust, so burning them was an attack on the system of exploitation.

topics.title: Ryotwari, Ricardo and the debt trap

learn.hook: In the Bombay Deccan, the Company dealt directly with each ryot and resurveyed lands every 30 years. Sounds fair? Not when the demand was too high!
points: After the Bengal experience, a different system was introduced in the Bombay Deccan in the 1820s: the ryotwari settlement, made directly with the ryot. The average income from different types of soil was estimated, the ryot's revenue-paying capacity assessed and a proportion fixed as the state's share. Lands were resurveyed every 30 years and revenue rates increased. The demand was not permanent.

Officials were influenced by the economist David Ricardo, who argued that a landowner should have a claim only to the 'average rent' prevailing at a given time. When land yielded more than this, the surplus should be taxed by the state; otherwise cultivators would become rentiers and not invest productively. Many officials thought Bengal's ryots had turned into rentiers, confirming Ricardo's theory.

The first revenue settlement in the Bombay Deccan was so high that in many places peasants deserted their villages and migrated to new regions, especially in areas of poor soil and fluctuating rainfall. When rains failed and harvests were poor, peasants could not pay; collectors, keen to show efficiency, seized property and imposed fines.
In the 1830s, agricultural prices fell sharply and did not recover for about fifteen years, cutting peasants' incomes further. Famine also struck the countryside.

To pay revenue and meet everyday and production needs, ryots borrowed from moneylenders. Once taken, loans were hard to repay; as debts mounted, ryots became dependent on moneylenders. By the 1840s officials found alarming levels of peasant indebtedness everywhere.

example.q: How did a Deccan ryot fall into a debt trap?
steps: Revenue demand was high and had to be paid even in bad years.
Prices fell in the 1830s, reducing income.
The ryot borrowed from the moneylender to pay revenue and buy necessities.
Interest piled up and the loan could not be repaid.
So he became dependent on the moneylender.
example.answer: High revenue and falling prices forced borrowing; mounting interest made repayment impossible, trapping him in debt.

learn.reallife: Microfinance and Kisan Credit Cards aim to give Indian farmers cheaper formal credit so they do not fall into the hands of high-interest moneylenders.

topics.title: The cotton boom and bust

learn.hook: When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, cotton from India suddenly became gold. Then the war ended, and the boom collapsed!
points: Before the 1860s, three-fourths of the raw cotton imports into Britain came from America. British cotton manufacturers, worried about this dependence, formed bodies like the Cotton Supply Association (1857) and the Manchester Cotton Company (1859) to encourage cotton cultivation elsewhere, including India.
When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, raw cotton imports from America fell to less than three per cent of the normal. By 1862 over 90 per cent of cotton imports into Britain came from India.

In the Bombay Deccan, credit flowed freely: export merchants in Bombay advanced money to urban sahukars, who extended credit to rural moneylenders, who lent to ryots. Ryots expanded cotton cultivation. Rich peasants gained, but most cotton ryots got deeper into debt.

When the Civil War ended in 1865, cotton production in America revived and Indian cotton exports to Britain declined steadily. Export merchants and sahukars were no longer keen to give long-term credit; moneylenders refused loans to ryots.
At the same time, the next revenue settlement increased the demand dramatically, by 50 to 100 per cent. Ryots were squeezed from both sides: no credit and higher revenue.

example.q: Trace the chain of credit during the cotton boom.
steps: Bombay export merchants advanced money to urban sahukars.
Urban sahukars extended credit to rural moneylenders.
Rural moneylenders lent to ryots.
Ryots expanded cotton cultivation.
example.answer: Export merchants → urban sahukars → rural moneylenders → ryots.

topics.title: The experience of injustice: Limitation Law and petitions

learn.hook: A law meant to protect ryots from endless interest ended up trapping them further, because moneylenders made them sign a fresh bond every three years!
points: Ryots were angry when moneylenders refused loans after the cotton boom. They were also angry that moneylenders violated customary norms. One norm was that the interest charged could not be more than the principal; under colonial rule this broke down, and in one case a moneylender charged over ₹2,000 as interest on a loan of ₹100.

In 1859 the British passed a Limitation Law stating that loan bonds signed between moneylenders and ryots would be valid for only three years. The law was meant to check the accumulation of interest over time.

Moneylenders manipulated the law by forcing the ryot to sign a new bond every three years. The unpaid balance, the original loan plus accumulated interest, was entered as the principal of the new bond, and new interest was charged on it.

Ryots' petitions complained that moneylenders refused to give receipts for repayments, entered fictitious figures in bonds, acquired the peasants' harvest at low prices and finally took over their property.
Most ryots were illiterate and did not know what they were signing. Deeds and bonds thus became symbols of a new oppressive system, which explains why, in 1875, ryots burnt them.

example.q: Explain how moneylenders manipulated the Limitation Law.
steps: The law made bonds valid for only three years.
Moneylenders made ryots sign a new bond every three years.
Unpaid loan plus interest became the new principal.
New interest was charged on this bigger sum, so debts grew.
example.answer: By renewing bonds every three years with interest added to the principal, so the law that was meant to limit interest actually increased debts.

learn.reallife: Today, laws against usury and state Money-Lenders Acts in Maharashtra and other states cap interest rates and require licences for moneylenders.

topics.title: The Deccan Riots Commission and reading official records

learn.hook: An official commission studied the riots and concluded: 'Government revenue is not to blame; the moneylenders are.' Would a government ever blame itself?
points: When the revolt spread in the Deccan, the Bombay government was initially unconcerned. But the Government of India, worried by the memory of 1857, pressured it to set up a commission of enquiry. The commission's report, the Deccan Riots Report, was presented to the British Parliament in 1878.

The commission held enquiries in the districts where the riots had spread, recorded statements of ryots, sahukars and eyewitnesses, compiled statistics on revenue rates, prices and interest rates in different regions, and collated reports from district collectors.

The commission was mainly interested in whether the level of government revenue demand caused the revolt. After examining the evidence, it reported that the government demand was not the cause of peasant anger; it blamed the moneylenders.

This shows the colonial government's reluctance to admit that popular discontent was ever caused by its own actions. Official reports are invaluable sources, but they must be read carefully and juxtaposed with evidence from newspapers, unofficial accounts, legal records and, where possible, oral sources.

Timeline: 1765 Company acquires Diwani of Bengal; 1773 Regulating Act; 1793 Permanent Settlement; around 1800 Santhals come to the Rajmahal hills; 1820s ryotwari in the Bombay Deccan; 1855–56 Santhal hul; 1861 cotton boom begins; 1875 Deccan riots; 1878 Deccan Riots Report.

example.q: Why did the Deccan Riots Commission blame moneylenders rather than revenue demand?
steps: The commission was set up by the colonial government.
Admitting that revenue caused the revolt would blame the government itself.
So it concluded that moneylenders were responsible.
Historians therefore read such reports critically alongside other evidence.
example.answer: Because the colonial government was reluctant to admit its own policies caused discontent; this is why such reports must be read critically.

learn.reallife: Commissions of inquiry are still set up in India after major events; journalists and researchers routinely compare their findings with other evidence.

chapters.title: Part III: Rebels and the Raj: The 1857 Revolt and its Representations

topics.title: Meerut to Delhi: the revolt begins

learn.hook: On the afternoon of 10 May 1857, sepoys at Meerut rose in mutiny. By the next morning they were at the gates of the Red Fort, asking the old Mughal emperor to lead them!
points: On the afternoon of 10 May 1857, a mutiny broke out in the cantonment of Meerut. It started with the sepoys of the native infantry, spread to the cavalry and then to the city. Ordinary people of the town and nearby villages joined the sepoys.
The sepoys captured the bell of arms (the arsenal), attacked white people, and plundered and set fire to their bungalows and records.
Late at night a group of sepoys rode to Delhi, arriving at the gates of the Red Fort early on 11 May. They demanded that the Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah, give them his blessings.
The emperor, old and with only a nominal court, was not happy at first, but eventually agreed to become the nominal leader of the rebellion.

This gave the revolt legitimacy: it could now be carried out in the name of the Mughal emperor, whose name still carried great prestige across north India. When the news spread that Delhi had fallen, mutinies broke out in cantonments across the Ganga valley and to the west of Delhi.

example.q: Why was the Mughal emperor important to the rebels?
steps: The Mughal name carried centuries of prestige.
The emperor's blessing gave the revolt legitimacy.
Rebels could claim to fight for a recognised sovereign, not just as mutineers.
This helped bring together different groups under one symbol.
example.answer: Because the emperor's name gave the revolt legitimacy and a unifying symbol across north India.

learn.reallife: Meerut has a Shaheed Smarak (martyrs' memorial) and a freedom struggle museum that recall the events of 10 May 1857.

topics.title: How the mutinies began: signals and targets

learn.hook: In cantonment after cantonment, the revolt started with a signal: the evening gun or a bugle call. Then the targets were always the same.
points: In every cantonment, sepoys began their action with a signal: the firing of the evening gun or the sounding of the bugle.
They first seized the bell of arms and plundered the treasury.
They then attacked government buildings: the jail, treasury, telegraph office, record room and bungalows, burning all records.

Everything and everybody connected with the white man became a target. Proclamations in Hindi, Urdu and Persian appealed to the population, both Hindus and Muslims, to unite and eliminate the firangis (foreigners).
Ordinary people joined the revolt and attacks spread to others seen as allies of the British, such as moneylenders and the rich in some places.

example.q: Why did rebels target treasuries, jails, telegraph offices and record rooms?
steps: Treasuries and arsenals gave money and weapons.
Jails and courts were symbols of British power.
Telegraph offices were key to British communication.
Records held revenue and debt details used to control people.
example.answer: Because these were the sources of British money, weapons, control and communication, and symbols of their rule.

learn.reallife: The British built the Mutiny Memorial on Delhi's Ridge in 1863; in 1972 India renamed it Ajitgarh and added a plaque honouring the Indian fighters of 1857.

topics.title: Lines of communication and sepoy panchayats

learn.hook: Sepoy panchayats met at night in the Kanpur lines. Far from being random, the revolt showed planning and collective decisions!
points: The sequence of events in different cantonments was similar, suggesting planning and coordination. Sepoys or their emissaries carried messages from one station to another.

A story from Awadh shows this: Captain Hearsey of the Awadh Military Police was protected by his Indian subordinates during the mutiny. The 41st Native Infantry, stationed nearby, insisted that since they had killed all their white officers, the Military Police should also kill Hearsey or hand him over. The Military Police refused.
It was decided that the matter would be resolved by a panchayat composed of native officers drawn from each regiment.
Charles Ball, who wrote one of the earliest histories of the revolt, noted that panchayats were convened nightly in the Kanpur sepoy lines. Decisions were taken collectively.
Sepoys lived together in the lines and shared a lifestyle; many came from the same caste and region. This made it natural for them to come together and decide their own future.

example.q: How did the rebels communicate and organise?
steps: Emissaries carried messages between stations.
Similar patterns in different places suggest coordination.
Sepoy panchayats of native officers took collective decisions.
Shared life in the lines and common backgrounds helped them organise.
example.answer: Through messengers between cantonments and through sepoy panchayats that took collective decisions.

learn.reallife: The word 'panchayat' is familiar to every Indian; in 1857 even soldiers used this village institution to make collective decisions.

topics.title: Leaders and followers

learn.hook: A Peshwa's adopted son, a queen, an elderly zamindar, a begum, a village leader, a wandering maulvi with a drum and a tribal cultivator: 1857 had leaders of every kind!
points: At Kanpur, Nana Sahib, the adopted son of the late Peshwa Baji Rao II, gathered armed forces, expelled the British garrison, proclaimed himself Peshwa and declared that he was a governor under Emperor Bahadur Shah.

At Lucknow, Birjis Qadr, the young son of the deposed Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, was declared the new Nawab; his mother, Begum Hazrat Mahal, took an active part in organising the uprising. At Jhansi, Rani Lakshmibai assumed leadership. In Bihar, Kunwar Singh, a local zamindar of Arrah, led the revolt.

Local leaders emerged too. Shah Mal of Baraut pargana (western Uttar Pradesh) mobilised the headmen and cultivators of 84 villages, moving from village to village at night. His men attacked government buildings, destroyed a bridge and dug up metalled roads; he turned an English officer's bungalow into a 'hall of justice'. He was killed in battle in July 1857.

Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah of Faizabad prophesied the end of British rule and fought the British in Lucknow and Awadh. He came to be known as Danka Shah, the maulvi with the drum. Gonoo, a tribal cultivator of Singhbhum in Chotanagpur, became a rebel leader of the Kol tribals.
Map work: centres of the revolt include Meerut, Delhi, Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Arrah and Bareilly. From Bareilly, the soldier Bakht Khan led a large force to Delhi.

example.q: Why did the revolt need both big leaders and local leaders?
steps: Big leaders (Nana Sahib, Rani Lakshmibai, Begum Hazrat Mahal) gave legitimacy and command in major centres.
Local leaders (Shah Mal, Gonoo) mobilised villagers and tribals.
Local leaders understood local grievances and terrain.
Together they spread the revolt widely.
example.answer: Big leaders provided legitimacy and command; local leaders mobilised ordinary people, so the revolt spread widely.

learn.reallife: Rani Lakshmibai's statue stands in Jhansi, and Begum Hazrat Mahal Park in Lucknow honours her role; Kunwar Singh is remembered across Bihar as 'Veer Kunwar Singh'.

topics.title: Rumours and prophecies

learn.hook: A low-caste worker at Dum Dum taunted a Brahmin sepoy who refused him water: 'You will soon lose your caste, for you will have to bite cartridges covered with the fat of cows and pigs!' The rumour spread like wildfire.
points: Rumours played a big role. The sepoys at Meerut and elsewhere believed that the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle were greased with the fat of cows and pigs, and that biting them would corrupt their caste and religion.

Captain Wright's report (January 1857) traced one source: at Dum Dum, near Calcutta, a low-caste khalasi asked a Brahmin sepoy for water from his lota; when refused, he said the sepoy would soon lose his caste by biting cartridges greased with cow and pig fat.

Another rumour said the British had mixed the bone dust of cows and pigs into the flour sold in the market. In towns and cantonments people refused to touch the atta. A prophecy said British rule would end on the centenary of the Battle of Plassey, 23 June 1857. Chapatis were also being distributed from village to village.

Rumours spread because they resonated with deeper fears. Since the late 1820s, under Lord William Bentinck, the British had promoted Western education, Western ideas and institutions, and laws abolishing sati (1829) and permitting the remarriage of Hindu widows (1856).

The British also annexed states on the plea of misgovernment and through the Doctrine of Lapse. Many people feared that everything they cherished, including their religion and social customs, was being destroyed and that Christianity would be imposed.

example.q: Why did people believe the rumours about greased cartridges and bone dust?
steps: They fitted fears created by British reforms like the abolition of sati and widow remarriage law.
Annexations through the Doctrine of Lapse showed the British could take away rulers' rights.
Missionary activity raised fears of forced conversion.
So the rumours seemed to confirm what people already feared.
example.answer: Because they matched widespread fears that the British were destroying Indian religion and customs.

learn.reallife: Fact-checking units in India today counter fake news on WhatsApp, a reminder that rumours spread fastest when they confirm people's fears.

topics.title: Awadh: 'a cherry that will drop into our mouth'

learn.hook: In 1851 Lord Dalhousie called Awadh 'a cherry that will drop into our mouth one day'. Five years later the British annexed it, and Awadh became the heart of the revolt.
points: In 1851 Governor-General Lord Dalhousie described the kingdom of Awadh as 'a cherry that will drop into our mouth one day'. Five years later, in 1856, it was formally annexed.

The process had begun earlier: the Subsidiary Alliance was imposed on Awadh in 1801. In 1856, Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was dethroned and exiled to Calcutta on the plea that the region was being misgoverned.

The British wrongly assumed the Nawab was unpopular. He was widely loved, and many followed him all the way to Kanpur singing songs of lament: 'Angrez Bahadur ain, mulk lai linho' (the Englishmen have come and taken the country).

The taluqdars of Awadh, local landholders with forts and armed retainers, were disarmed and their forts destroyed. The Summary Settlement of 1856, based on the assumption that taluqdars were interlopers with no permanent stake in the land, removed them wherever possible and gave the land to the peasants.

Before annexation, taluqdars held 67 per cent of the villages of Awadh; after the Summary Settlement, this fell to 38 per cent. Peasants did not gain much either: revenue was over-assessed and their insecurity grew.

example.q: How did the annexation of Awadh create widespread resentment?
steps: The popular Nawab was dethroned and exiled.
Taluqdars were disarmed and lost their lands.
Peasants faced over-assessed revenue.
So nobles, landholders and peasants all had grievances.
example.answer: It hurt the Nawab's supporters, the taluqdars and the peasants alike, uniting many groups against the British.

learn.reallife: Lucknow's culture of music, kathak, poetry and Awadhi cuisine, which flourished under Wajid Ali Shah, is still celebrated; he took this culture with him to Matiaburj in Kolkata.

topics.title: Awadh in revolt: courtiers, sepoys and peasants together

learn.hook: Awadh was called the 'nursery of the Bengal Army'. When its villages suffered, its sepoys felt it, and the revolt became a people's war.
points: The removal of the Nawab led to the dissolution of the court and its culture. A whole range of people lost their livelihood: musicians, dancers, poets, cooks, retainers and administrative officials.
Taluqdars, deprived of land and power, and peasants, burdened by over-assessed revenue, shared grievances. In many places taluqdars and peasants fought together against the British.

A large number of sepoys of the Bengal Army were recruited from the villages of Awadh, which was called the 'nursery of the Bengal Army'. For decades sepoys had complained about low pay and the difficulty of getting leave.

The sepoys' grievances merged with the grievances of their families and villages. Sepoys were linked to peasants by ties of kinship, so news of distress at home reached the lines, and the anger of the countryside reached the army.
That is why the revolt in Awadh became particularly widespread: it was a popular rebellion in which sepoys, taluqdars, peasants and the dependants of the old court all took part.

example.q: Why was the revolt particularly widespread in Awadh?
steps: The popular Nawab's removal hurt courtiers, artists and officials.
Taluqdars lost lands and forts; peasants faced high revenue.
Many sepoys came from Awadh villages and shared their families' grievances.
So almost every section of society had reasons to rebel.
example.answer: Because grievances of the court's dependants, taluqdars, peasants and sepoys all came together in Awadh.

learn.reallife: Lucknow's Residency ruins, with cannon-ball marks still visible, preserve the memory of the long siege during the revolt.

topics.title: What the rebels wanted

learn.hook: British accounts called the rebels mere mutineers. But their own proclamations tell a different story, of grievances, unity and a different idea of rule.
points: The rebels' own proclamations and messages are key sources for understanding their vision, since most other accounts were written by the British.

The proclamations in the name of Bahadur Shah appealed to all sections regardless of caste and creed, calling people to join the fight under the standards of both Muhammad and Mahavir. Hindu–Muslim unity was striking; British attempts to create divisions, such as spending money in Bareilly to incite Hindus against Muslims, failed.

The proclamations attacked symbols of British rule: land revenue settlements that had dispossessed landholders, foreign commerce that had ruined artisans and weavers, the threat to religion through Christianity, and moneylenders seen as allies of the British.

The Azamgarh Proclamation of 25 August 1857 listed grievances of different groups: zamindars (high revenue assessments), merchants (taxes and Company monopoly of trade), public servants (no high posts and low salaries for Indians), artisans (English goods causing unemployment), and pundits and fakirs (British hostility to Hindu and Muslim religions).

Where British rule collapsed, rebels in Delhi, Lucknow and Kanpur tried to set up an administration modelled on the eighteenth-century Mughal world: they made appointments to administrative and military posts, collected land revenue, paid troops and issued orders to stop looting. These structures were mainly for the needs of war and did not last.

example.q: Using the Azamgarh Proclamation, show what different groups resented about British rule.
steps: Zamindars: high revenue assessments.
Merchants: taxes and Company monopoly of trade.
Public servants: no high posts, low salaries.
Artisans: unemployment from English goods.
Pundits and fakirs: hostility to their religions.
example.answer: Each group had specific economic or religious grievances, which the proclamation brought together against British rule.

learn.reallife: The Indian Postal Department issued stamps honouring 1857 leaders, and the 150th anniversary in 2007 was marked as a celebration of the 'First War of Independence'.

topics.title: Repression

learn.hook: In 1857, laws were passed under which even ordinary Britons could try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion, and death was the only punishment.
points: Before sending troops, the British passed a series of laws. By Acts passed in May and June 1857, the whole of north India was put under martial law, and military officers and even ordinary Britons were given the power to try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion.
The ordinary processes of law and trial were suspended, and it was made clear that rebellion had only one punishment: death.

Reinforcements were brought from Britain. Delhi was recaptured after a two-pronged attack, one from Calcutta and the other from Punjab; the attempt began in June 1857, but the city was captured only in late September.
In the Gangetic plain the British advanced slowly, recapturing territory village by village. Punishments were harsh: rebels were hanged or blown from cannon in public, and villages were burnt.

In Awadh, the British also used diplomacy to break the unity of the rebels. They promised big landholders that their estates would be returned. Rebel landholders who did not submit were dispossessed, while loyal ones were rewarded.

example.q: How did the British suppress the revolt?
steps: Passed laws giving officers and Britons power to try and punish rebels; death the only punishment.
Brought reinforcements and recaptured Delhi in September 1857.
Advanced village by village with harsh punishments: hangings, blowing from cannon, burning villages.
In Awadh, won back taluqdars by promising to restore their estates.
example.answer: Through harsh laws, military force, public terror and a policy of winning back taluqdars.

learn.reallife: Jallianwala Bagh (1919) and other later events show that colonial repression continued; memorials across India today recall these moments.

topics.title: The revolt in images: celebrating the avengers and the honour of Britain

learn.hook: British paintings showed their generals as saviours and English women as innocent victims. Images were weapons too, shaping how people in Britain felt about 1857.
points: Pictures, paintings, cartoons and popular prints produced by the British and by Indians are important sources. They show how the revolt was represented and remembered, and how images shaped public opinion.

British paintings celebrated those who saved the English and repressed the rebels. 'Relief of Lucknow', painted by Thomas Jones Barker in 1859, shows the moment the British commander Colin Campbell arrived at the Lucknow Residency and was greeted by James Outram and Henry Havelock.

During the siege, Henry Lawrence, the Commissioner of Lucknow, had gathered the Christian population in the fortified Residency. Lawrence was killed, but the siege continued; Outram and Havelock cut through the rebel forces to reinforce the garrison, and later Colin Campbell's forces rescued it. In British accounts they became heroes.

Images of English women and children were used to show the 'honour of Britain' under threat. 'In Memoriam' by Joseph Noel Paton shows English women and children huddled together, helpless and innocent, as if awaiting dishonour and death, stirring anger and grief in Britain.
Other images showed English women as heroic defenders. A print of Miss Wheeler at Kanpur shows her defending herself single-handedly against rebels, presented as protecting her honour.

example.q: What purpose did paintings like 'Relief of Lucknow' and 'In Memoriam' serve in Britain?
steps: 'Relief of Lucknow' glorified British commanders as rescuers.
'In Memoriam' showed English women and children as helpless victims.
Both stirred emotions of pride, grief and anger.
They built public support for harsh repression.
example.answer: They glorified British heroes, portrayed the English as victims and stirred public feeling in favour of revenge and repression.

learn.reallife: Indian films and TV serials about 1857, like 'Manikarnika' (2019), also use images to shape how audiences feel about history.

topics.title: Retribution, terror and 'Clemency Canning'

learn.hook: When Lord Canning urged leniency, the British press mocked him as 'Clemency Canning'. The mood in Britain was revenge, not mercy.
points: As news of the revolt reached Britain, there were demands for retribution and revenge. Images expressed this mood.

'Justice', an allegorical image by John Tenniel published in the magazine Punch in September 1857, showed a fierce female figure of Justice with sword and shield, attacking rebels while Indian women and children cowered in fear. It expressed the demand for vengeance.

Terror was displayed openly. Rebels were executed in public, blown from cannons and hanged from gallows, and images of these punishments were widely circulated in popular journals. The aim was to create fear and discourage further rebellion.
Lord Canning, the Governor-General, declared that a soft line and gestures of clemency would help win back the loyalty of the sepoys.

The British press ridiculed him. A cartoon in Punch, 'The Clemency of Canning', showed him as a benign figure patting the head of a sepoy who still held a bloodied sword. He was mocked as 'Clemency Canning', showing there was no time for mercy in British public opinion.

example.q: What do images like 'Justice' and 'The Clemency of Canning' tell us about British public opinion?
steps: 'Justice' showed the demand for vengeance.
Public executions were shown to spread terror.
'The Clemency of Canning' mocked any idea of mercy.
So British opinion was dominated by anger and the desire for revenge.
example.answer: That British public opinion demanded harsh retribution and scorned leniency.

learn.reallife: Political cartoons remain powerful in India: R.K. Laxman's 'Common Man' in The Times of India commented on public life for over five decades.

topics.title: Nationalist imagery and reading the sources of 1857

learn.hook: 'Khoob ladi mardani woh to Jhansi wali rani thi.' Subhadra Kumari Chauhan's poem made generations of Indian children see Rani Lakshmibai as a fearless warrior.
points: In the twentieth century, the nationalist movement drew inspiration from 1857. A whole world of nationalist imagination was woven around the revolt. It was celebrated as the First War of Independence, in which people of all classes came together to fight colonial rule; V.D. Savarkar wrote of it in this way.

Art and literature helped keep the memory alive. Rani Lakshmibai was portrayed as a heroic, masculine figure chasing the enemy, slaying British soldiers and fighting bravely till the last. Popular prints showed her on horseback, sword in one hand, reins in the other.
Children grew up reading Subhadra Kumari Chauhan's poem with the lines 'Khoob ladi mardani woh to Jhansi wali rani thi' (Like a man, she fought valiantly, the Rani of Jhansi).

Historians compare different visual representations: British images glorified rescuers, portrayed English women as victims and demanded revenge; nationalist images glorified rebel leaders and presented the revolt as a war of independence.

Timeline: 1801 Subsidiary Alliance imposed on Awadh; 1856 Awadh annexed; 10 May 1857 mutiny at Meerut; late September 1857 Delhi recaptured; June 1858 Rani Lakshmibai killed in battle; 1858 an Act of the British Parliament ended Company rule and transferred power to the British Crown.

example.q: What do visual representations tell us about the revolt of 1857?
steps: British images showed British heroes, English women as victims and demanded revenge.
Nationalist images showed rebels like Rani Lakshmibai as heroic freedom fighters.
Both used images to shape emotions and memory.
So images tell us about how different people remembered and interpreted 1857.
example.answer: They reveal how British and Indian audiences interpreted the revolt, each through its own concerns.

learn.reallife: Rani Lakshmibai's name lives on in the Rani Lakshmi Bai Central Agricultural University in Jhansi and the Rani Jhansi Regiment of Netaji's INA during the Second World War.

chapters.title: Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement: Civil Disobedience and Beyond

topics.title: A leader announces himself

learn.hook: In January 1915 a lawyer returned to India after two decades in South Africa. Within a few years, he would change the meaning of Indian nationalism.
points: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned to India in January 1915 after two decades in South Africa, where he had gone as a lawyer and become a leader of the Indian community.

It was in South Africa that he first forged the distinctive technique of non-violent protest known as satyagraha, first promoted harmony between religions, and first alerted upper-caste Indians to their discriminatory treatment of low castes and women. The historian Chandran Devanesan remarked that South Africa was 'the making of the Mahatma'.

The India of 1915 was very different from the India of 1893. The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, now had branches in most major cities and towns. Through the Swadeshi movement of 1905–07 it had broadened its appeal among the middle classes.

That movement produced major leaders: Bal Gangadhar Tilak of Maharashtra, Bipin Chandra Pal of Bengal and Lala Lajpat Rai of Punjab ('Lal, Bal and Pal'), who advocated militant opposition to colonial rule. 'Moderates' like Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Mohammad Ali Jinnah preferred a gradual and persuasive approach.
On the advice of his political mentor Gokhale, Gandhi spent a year travelling around British India, getting to know the land and its peoples.

example.q: Why did Gokhale advise Gandhi to travel through British India first?
steps: Gandhi had been away for two decades.
India and its politics had changed greatly.
Travelling would help him understand the land and its peoples.
This knowledge would help him lead a mass movement.
example.answer: So that Gandhi could understand India and its people before taking a leading role.

learn.reallife: The Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, celebrated on 9 January, marks the day Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in 1915.

topics.title: Banaras speech and the first satyagrahas

learn.hook: At the opening of Banaras Hindu University in 1916, Gandhi told jewel-laden princes that India's salvation would come through its farmers, not its lawyers, doctors or rich landlords!
points: Gandhi's first major public appearance was at the opening of the Banaras Hindu University (BHU) in February 1916. The invitees included princes and philanthropists whose donations had helped found BHU.

Gandhi charged the Indian elite with a lack of concern for the labouring poor. He said there was no salvation for India unless the wealthy held their riches in trust for their countrymen, and that 'our salvation can only come through the farmers', not through lawyers, doctors or rich landlords.
The speech showed that Indian nationalism was still an elite phenomenon, a creation of lawyers, doctors and landlords, and that Gandhi wanted to make it representative of the whole Indian people.

In December 1916, at the Congress session in Lucknow, a peasant from Champaran in Bihar told Gandhi about the harsh treatment of peasants by British indigo planters. In 1917 Gandhi spent much time in Champaran, seeking security of tenure for the peasants and the freedom to cultivate crops of their choice.

In 1918 he was involved in two campaigns in Gujarat: a labour dispute in Ahmedabad, demanding better working conditions for textile mill workers, and in Kheda, asking the state to remit taxes after the failure of the harvest. These campaigns established Gandhi as a nationalist with deep sympathy for the poor.

example.q: How did the Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda campaigns build Gandhi's reputation?
steps: Champaran: for indigo peasants' rights.
Ahmedabad: for mill workers' conditions.
Kheda: for tax remission after crop failure.
Each took up the cause of poor people, showing his concern for them.
example.answer: By championing peasants and workers in all three, they established him as a leader who cared for the poor.

learn.reallife: The centenary of the Champaran Satyagraha was celebrated across Bihar in 2017, a hundred years after Gandhi took up the indigo peasants' cause.

topics.title: The Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh

learn.hook: Punjab's soldiers had fought for Britain in the First World War. Their reward? A law allowing detention without trial, and then the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh.
points: During the First World War (1914–18), the British had instituted censorship of the press and permitted detention without trial. On the recommendation of a committee chaired by Sir Sidney Rowlatt, these tough measures were continued after the war. This was the Rowlatt Act of 1919.

Gandhi called for a countrywide campaign against the Rowlatt Act. In towns across north and west India, life came to a standstill as shops shut down and schools closed in response to the call for a hartal (bandh).
The protests were particularly intense in Punjab, where many men had served on the British side in the war and expected to be rewarded. Instead they got the Rowlatt Act.

Gandhi was detained while on his way to Punjab, and prominent local Congressmen were arrested. The situation escalated, and in April 1919 at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, a British Brigadier ordered his troops to open fire on a nationalist meeting. More than four hundred people were killed in this massacre.
It was the Rowlatt satyagraha that made Gandhi a truly national leader.

example.q: Why were protests against the Rowlatt Act especially intense in Punjab?
steps: Many Punjabi men had served in the British army in the First World War.
They expected to be rewarded after the war.

topics.title: Non-cooperation and Khilafat

learn.hook: 'Non-cooperation became the name of an epoch in the life of India and of Gandhi,' wrote Louis Fischer. Students, lawyers, workers, tribals and peasants all joined in!
points: After Jallianwala Bagh, Gandhi called for a campaign of non-cooperation with British rule, launched in 1920. Indians who wished colonialism to end were asked to stop attending schools, colleges and law courts and not to pay taxes. They were asked to renounce all voluntary association with the British government, including giving up titles. Gandhi said that if non-cooperation was carried out effectively, India would win swaraj within a year.

To broaden the struggle, Gandhi joined hands with the Khilafat Movement, led by Muslim leaders such as Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, which sought to defend the position of the Khalifa (Caliph), the Ottoman Sultan of Turkey, and restore his authority after the First World War. Gandhi hoped this would bring Hindus and Muslims together.

Students stopped going to government schools and colleges. Lawyers refused to attend court. Foreign cloth was boycotted and burnt in bonfires. The working class went on strike in many towns and cities: according to official figures there were 396 strikes involving 6,00,000 workers in 1921.

The countryside was seething: hill tribes in northern Andhra violated forest laws; farmers in Awadh did not pay taxes; peasants in Kumaun refused to carry loads for colonial officials. These protests were sometimes carried out in defiance of the local nationalist leadership.

As the American biographer Louis Fischer wrote, 'Non-cooperation became the name of an epoch in the life of India and of Gandhiji.' It was negative enough to be peaceful but positive enough to be effective.

example.q: How did the Non-Cooperation Movement become a form of protest that reached many groups?
steps: Students boycotted government schools and colleges.
Lawyers boycotted courts; titles were renounced.

Tribals defied forest laws and peasants refused taxes and forced labour.
example.answer: By giving every group a way to withdraw cooperation, from boycotting schools and courts to strikes and defying forest and tax laws.

topics.title: Chauri Chaura and Gandhi's trial

learn.hook: After a mob burnt a police station at Chauri Chaura in 1922, Gandhi called off a nationwide movement at its height. Then a British judge told him he was 'a great patriot'!
points: In February 1922, a group of peasants attacked and torched a police station in the hamlet of Chauri Chaura in the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh). Several constables perished in the fire.
This act of violence prompted Gandhi to call off the Non-Cooperation Movement altogether. He said that no provocation could justify the brutal murder of men who had been rendered defenceless.
During the movement, thousands of Indians were put in jail. Gandhi himself was arrested in March 1922 and charged with sedition.

The judge who presided over his trial, Justice C.N. Broomfield, made a remarkable speech while sentencing him. He said that Gandhi was in a different category from anyone he had ever tried; that in the eyes of millions he was a great patriot and leader; and that even those who differed with him saw him as a man of high ideals and noble, even saintly, life.
Since Gandhi had violated the law, the Bench was obliged to sentence him, and he was sentenced to six years' imprisonment.

example.q: Why did Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement after Chauri Chaura?
steps: The movement was based on non-violence.
At Chauri Chaura, a mob killed defenceless policemen.
Gandhi felt no provocation could justify such violence.
He believed the people were not yet ready for non-violent mass struggle, so he called it off.
example.answer: Because the violence at Chauri Chaura went against the principle of non-violence on which the movement was based.

learn.reallife: A memorial at Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur district was built to remember the events of 1922; the centenary was observed in 2021–22.

topics.title: A people's leader

learn.hook: In villages of eastern UP, rumours said that anyone who spoke against 'Gandhi baba' would see their house collapse or their crops fail. Peasants saw him as more than a politician!
points: By 1922, Gandhi had transformed Indian nationalism. It was no longer a movement of professionals and intellectuals; hundreds of thousands of peasants, workers and artisans participated. Many venerated him as their 'Mahatma'.

Gandhi dressed like ordinary people, lived like them and spoke their language. Unlike other leaders, he did not stand apart from the common folk but identified with them. He was often seen in a simple dhoti.

He spent part of each day working on the charkha (spinning wheel) and encouraged other nationalists to do the same. Spinning helped him break the traditional boundaries between mental labour and manual labour.

The historian Shahid Amin traced the image of Gandhi among peasants in eastern Uttar Pradesh, as reported in the local press. Rumours spread of his miraculous powers: that he had been sent by the King to redress the grievances of farmers, that he could overrule local officials, and that those who opposed him would suffer misfortunes.
Peasants knew him as 'Gandhi baba', 'Gandhi Maharaj' or simply 'Mahatma'. To them he was a saviour who would rescue them from high taxes and oppressive officials, and restore their dignity.

example.q: How did Gandhi identify with the common people?
steps: He dressed simply, in a dhoti.

example.answer: Through his simple dress and lifestyle, use of their language, manual labour on the charkha and support for their causes.

topics.title: Constructive programme and the growth of the Congress

learn.hook: For Gandhi, freedom was not just about getting the British out. India also had to free itself of untouchability, child marriage and communal hatred.
points: Gandhi believed India would not be fit for swaraj unless it freed itself of social evils such as child marriage and untouchability. He worked to remove untouchability and promoted Hindu–Muslim harmony.

He promoted khadi (hand-spun, hand-woven cloth) as a means of economic self-reliance and as a symbol of the nation. The constructive programme included khadi, village industries, Hindu–Muslim unity and the abolition of untouchability.
Under Gandhi's leadership, new branches of the Congress were set up in various parts of India. A series of Praja Mandals was established to promote the nationalist creed in the princely states.

Gandhi encouraged communication in the mother tongue rather than English. Provincial Congress committees were based on linguistic regions rather than the artificial boundaries of British India. Nationalism thus reached the farthest corners of the country.

The movement also gained support from prosperous peasants and from industrialists, such as G.D. Birla, who supported the national movement. Gandhi had talented followers, including Mahadev Desai, Vallabhbhai Patel, J.B. Kripalani, Subhas Chandra Bose, Abul Kalam Azad, Jawaharlal Nehru, Sarojini Naidu, Govind Ballabh Pant and C. Rajagopalachari.

steps: New branches were set up across India.

example.answer: Through new branches, Praja Mandals, linguistic provincial committees and the use of mother tongues.

topics.title: Purna Swaraj and the choice of salt

learn.hook: Of all things, why salt? Because every household needed it, the British had a monopoly over it, and even the poorest paid a tax on it!
points: In 1928 the Simon Commission, sent by Britain to enquire into conditions in the colony, arrived in India. As it had no Indian members, it was boycotted with the slogan 'Simon go back'.
In December 1929 the Congress held its annual session in Lahore, with Jawaharlal Nehru as president. It declared its commitment to Purna Swaraj, complete independence.

On 26 January 1930, 'Independence Day' was observed: the national flag was hoisted at different venues and patriotic songs were sung. Gandhi gave precise instructions on how the day should be observed.
Soon after, Gandhi announced a march to break the salt law, one of the most widely disliked laws in British India. It gave the state a monopoly over the manufacture and sale of salt.

Salt was used in every Indian household, yet Indians were forbidden from making it even for domestic use and were compelled to buy it at a high price from shops. By targeting the salt monopoly, Gandhi hoped to mobilise a wider discontent against British rule, since the salt tax hurt everyone, rich and poor.

example.q: Why did the salt law become an important issue?

The British held a monopoly over its manufacture and sale.

example.answer: Because the tax on a universal necessity affected every Indian, making it a powerful symbol of unjust British rule.

topics.title: The Dandi March and Civil Disobedience

learn.hook: On 12 March 1930, Gandhi set out from Sabarmati with his followers. About three weeks later, at Dandi, he picked up a fistful of salt, and an empire trembled.
points: Gandhi notified the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, of his plan in advance, but Irwin failed to grasp the significance of the action.

On 12 March 1930 Gandhi began walking from his ashram at Sabarmati towards the ocean. He reached Dandi three weeks later and, on 6 April 1930, made a fistful of salt, thereby breaking the law. Parallel salt marches were held in other parts of the country.

This launched the Civil Disobedience Movement. Peasants breached forest laws; factory workers went on strike; lawyers boycotted British courts; and students refused to attend government-run educational institutions. Over 60,000 Indians were arrested, including Gandhi himself.

The march was significant for three reasons. First, it brought Gandhi to world attention: it was widely covered by the European and American press. Second, it was the first nationalist activity in which women participated in large numbers; the socialist activist Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay had persuaded Gandhi not to restrict the protests to men alone.
Third, the march forced the British to realise that their Raj would not last forever and that they would have to devolve some power to Indians.

example.q: What was the significance of the Salt March?
steps: It brought Gandhi to world attention through European and American press coverage.
Women participated in large numbers for the first time.
It made the British realise they would have to devolve power.

example.answer: It drew world attention, brought women into the movement and forced the British to see that their rule could not last.

learn.reallife: The National Salt Satyagraha Memorial at Dandi in Gujarat, opened in 2019, recreates the march with statues of Gandhi and the 80 marchers.

topics.title: Dialogues: Round Tables, the Irwin Pact and the Poona Pact

learn.hook: At the Second Round Table Conference in London, Gandhi claimed to speak for all of India. Three groups disagreed: the Muslim League, the princes and Dr B.R. Ambedkar.
points: The British began a series of Round Table Conferences in London. The first, in November 1930, was held without Gandhi, as the Congress boycotted it; it was futile.

Gandhi was released from jail in January 1931 and held long meetings with the Viceroy. These led to the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (March 1931): Civil Disobedience would be called off, all prisoners released and salt manufacture allowed along the coast. Radical nationalists criticised the pact because Gandhi did not get a commitment to political independence.

A Second Round Table Conference was held in London in the latter part of 1931, with Gandhi representing the Congress. His claim that the Congress represented all of India was challenged by the Muslim League (which claimed to stand for the Muslim minority), the princes (who said the Congress had no stake in their territories) and B.R. Ambedkar (who argued that Gandhi and the Congress did not truly represent the lowest castes). The conference was inconclusive, and Gandhi resumed civil disobedience on his return. The new Viceroy, Lord Willingdon, had no sympathy for him.
Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the depressed classes. Gandhi opposed this, fearing it would permanently divide them from Hindu society, and went on a fast.
The Poona Pact (1932) between Gandhi and Ambedkar resolved the issue: instead of separate electorates, seats were reserved for the depressed classes within the general electorate.

example.q: Why was Gandhi's claim to represent all of India challenged at the Second Round Table Conference?
steps: The Muslim League claimed to represent Muslims.
The princes said the Congress had no stake in their territories.
Ambedkar said the Congress did not represent the lowest castes.
So different groups contested the Congress's claim.
example.answer: Because the Muslim League, the princes and Ambedkar each claimed the Congress did not represent their group.

learn.reallife: Reserved seats for Scheduled Castes in Parliament and state assemblies today follow the principle agreed in the Poona Pact: reservation within joint electorates.

topics.title: Provincial ministries, war, Cripps and Quit India

learn.hook: 'Do or Die!' In August 1942 Gandhi gave this call, and within hours he and other leaders were in jail. Yet the movement raged on for over a year.
points: The Government of India Act of 1935 promised some form of representative government. In 1937, elections were held on a restricted franchise, and the Congress won a comprehensive victory: eight out of eleven provinces had a Congress 'Prime Minister' working under a British Governor.

In September 1939, two years after the Congress ministries took office, the Second World War broke out. Gandhi and Nehru were critical of Hitler and the Nazis and promised support if the British promised independence after the war. The offer was refused, and in protest the Congress ministries resigned in October 1939.

In 1942 Prime Minister Winston Churchill sent Sir Stafford Cripps to forge a compromise with Gandhi and the Congress. Talks broke down when the Congress insisted that, if it was to help defend India from the Axis powers, the Viceroy must first appoint an Indian as the Defence Member of his Executive Council.

After the failure of the Cripps Mission, Gandhi launched his third major movement, Quit India, in August 1942, with the call 'Do or Die'. Gandhi and other leaders were jailed at once, but younger activists organised strikes and acts of sabotage across the country. Socialist members of the Congress, such as Jayaprakash Narayan, were particularly active in the underground resistance.

In several districts, such as Satara in the west and Medinipur in the east, 'independent' governments were proclaimed. The British responded with great force, yet it took more than a year to suppress the rebellion. Quit India was a genuine mass movement involving hundreds of thousands of ordinary Indians.

example.q: Why did the Quit India Movement continue even after Gandhi and other leaders were jailed?
steps: Younger activists organised strikes and sabotage.
Socialists like Jayaprakash Narayan led underground resistance.
Parallel governments were set up in Satara and Medinipur.
Ordinary people in large numbers joined, making it a mass movement.
example.answer: Because younger and underground leaders and ordinary people carried it on, making it a genuine mass movement.

learn.reallife: 9 August is observed as August Kranti Din; the Gowalia Tank Maidan in Mumbai, where the Quit India call was given, is now called August Kranti Maidan.

topics.title: Towards independence: the League, Simla and the Cabinet Mission

learn.hook: In the 1946 elections, the Congress swept the general seats while the Muslim League won almost all seats reserved for Muslims. The political polarisation was complete.
points: In 1940 the Muslim League passed a resolution (the Lahore resolution) demanding a measure of autonomy for the Muslim-majority areas of the subcontinent, which came to be seen as a demand for Pakistan. During Quit India, while Congress leaders were in jail, the League worked to extend its influence, especially in Punjab and Sind.

In 1945 a Labour government came to power in Britain, committed to granting independence to India. The Viceroy, Lord Wavell, brought the Congress and the League together for talks, including the Simla conference of 1945, but no agreement was reached.
In early 1946 fresh elections were held to the provincial legislatures. The Congress swept the 'General' category, but in the seats reserved for Muslims the League won an overwhelming majority.

A Cabinet Mission came in the summer of 1946. It failed to get the Congress and the League to agree on a federal system that would keep India together while allowing the provinces a degree of autonomy.

After the talks broke down, Jinnah called for a 'Direct Action Day' on 16 August 1946 to press the League's demand for Pakistan. Bloody riots broke out in Calcutta that day and spread to rural Bengal, Bihar, the United Provinces and Punjab.

example.q: Why did the Cabinet Mission fail?
steps: It proposed a federal system keeping India together with provincial autonomy.
The Congress and the League could not agree on its terms.
Political polarisation after the 1946 elections made compromise harder.
So the talks broke down, followed by Direct Action Day.
example.answer: Because the Congress and the League, deeply polarised after the 1946 elections, could not agree on its federal plan.

learn.reallife: Historians in India and Pakistan continue to study the events of 1946–47; the Partition Museum in Amritsar records the experiences of people who lived through them.

topics.title: The last heroic days

learn.hook: On 15 August 1947, while Delhi celebrated, Gandhi was in Calcutta, fasting for 24 hours. For him, freedom without peace was incomplete.
points: On 15 August 1947 India became independent, but the joy was mixed with the pain of Partition and communal violence. Gandhi was not in Delhi for the celebrations; he was in Calcutta, where he did not attend any function or hoist a flag, and marked the day with a 24-hour fast.

Gandhi toured riot-torn areas: Noakhali in east Bengal, villages in Bihar, and the riot-torn slums of Calcutta and Delhi, trying to stop the violence and comfort the victims. He worked to ensure that minorities felt safe.
He fasted in Calcutta and in Delhi to restore communal peace. Through his efforts and persuasion, the Congress passed a resolution on the 'rights of minorities', promising to protect them.
On 30 January 1948, Gandhi was shot dead at his daily prayer meeting in Delhi by Nathuram Godse, who had denounced him as an 'appeaser' of Muslims.

His death led to an extraordinary outpouring of grief, with tributes from across the world. Time magazine compared his martyrdom to that of Abraham Lincoln: just as Lincoln had been killed for believing that people were equal regardless of race, Gandhi was killed for believing that friendship between Hindus and Muslims was possible and necessary. Timeline: 1915 return; 1917–18 Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad; 1919 Rowlatt satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh; 1920–22 Non-Cooperation; 1930 Salt March; 1942 Quit India; 1947 independence; 1948 assassination.

topics.title: Knowing Gandhi: sources and their limits

learn.hook: During the Salt March, police reports tried to show that it was failing, while Indian newspapers reported huge crowds. Same event, very different stories!
points: Historians use many sources to study Gandhi and the national movement: the writings and speeches of Gandhi and his contemporaries, including associates and opponents. It is important to distinguish between the public voice (speeches meant for audiences) and private scripts (personal letters and diaries).

Letters give a glimpse of private thoughts: anger, pain, hopes and frustrations. Gandhi regularly published letters others wrote to him in his journal Harijan. Nehru edited a collection of letters written to him during the national movement, A Bunch of Old Letters. But many letters were written knowing they might be published, so even 'private' letters may be shaped for the public.

Autobiographies, like Gandhi's My Experiments with Truth, are retrospective accounts, often written from memory. They tell us what the author remembered, saw as important and how they wanted their life to be viewed; they frame a picture, so we must read them carefully.

Government records are another source. The Home Department prepared fortnightly reports from the early twentieth century, based on police information from localities. These often expressed what higher officials wanted to believe: during the Salt March, they claimed it was not drawing much response, while evidence shows mass participation.

Newspapers, in English and in Indian languages, tracked Gandhi's movements and reported what ordinary people thought. But they were published by people with their own political views: a London newspaper and an Indian nationalist paper might describe the same event very differently. All sources must be read critically and compared.

example.q: How do private letters and autobiographies differ from official accounts as sources on Gandhi?
steps: Letters reveal personal thoughts and feelings, though some were written for publication.
Autobiographies show how the author wanted to be remembered.
Official reports reflect the government's views and interests.
So each has its own bias and must be compared with others.
example.answer: Letters and autobiographies show personal perspectives, while official accounts show the government's view; each must be read critically.

chapters.title: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era

topics.title: Framing the Constitution: an introduction

learn.hook: India's Constitution was not written in a day. It was argued over, clause by clause, for nearly three years by an Assembly representing a vast and divided country.
points: The Constitution of India came into effect on 26 January 1950. It is among the longest constitutions in the world, reflecting the country's size and diversity.

It was framed between December 1946 and November 1949. Drafts were discussed clause by clause in the Constituent Assembly over eleven sessions, with sittings spread over 165 days; between sessions, committees and sub-committees revised the drafts.
The Constituent Assembly Debates (CAD), the printed record of these discussions, run into eleven bulky volumes and are a major source for historians.

The Constitution was framed against a backdrop of deep diversity and division: a country of many religions, languages, castes and regions, recovering from colonial rule and torn by the violence of Partition. It had to bind together a diverse people and set out a democratic future.

Timeline: 26 July 1945 Labour government in Britain; December 1945–January 1946 general elections in India; 16 May 1946 Cabinet Mission announces its scheme; 16 August 1946 Direct Action Day; 9 December 1946 Constituent Assembly begins; 13 December 1946 Objectives Resolution; 15 August 1947 independence and partition; 26 November 1949 Constitution adopted; 26 January 1950 Constitution comes into effect.

example.q: Why are the Constituent Assembly Debates an important historical source?
steps: They record arguments of members clause by clause.
They show disagreements, compromises and reasons behind provisions.
They reveal the concerns of different groups in a divided society.
So they help us understand why the Constitution looks as it does.
example.answer: Because they record the arguments and compromises behind every provision, revealing how and why the Constitution was framed.

learn.reallife: India celebrates Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) on 26 November, the day the Constitution was adopted in 1949, and Republic Day on 26 January.

topics.title: A tumultuous time

learn.hook: The years before the Constitution saw a navy mutiny, a national army formed abroad, horrific riots and the partition of the country. The framers wrote with these fresh in their minds.
points: The years before the Constitution were tumultuous. The Quit India Movement of 1942 was the last mass movement against British rule. Subhas Chandra Bose had formed the Indian National Army (INA) to fight the British with armed struggle.

In the spring of 1946, ratings of the Royal Indian Navy (RIN) mutinied in Bombay and other cities, in sympathy with the INA and against British rule. There were strikes and protests by workers and peasants across the country.

There was also bitter communal conflict: the Great Calcutta Killings of August 1946 were followed by riots across north and east India, and then by the violence of Partition in 1947, which uprooted millions and killed hundreds of thousands.

Another major problem was the integration of the princely states. During the Raj, roughly one-third of the subcontinent's area was ruled by Nawabs and Maharajas who owed allegiance to the British Crown. At independence their status was uncertain, and some rulers dreamt of independence.
These experiences of violence and fragmentation shaped the framers' concerns: unity, stability, a strong centre and protection for all citizens.

example.q: How did the tumultuous events of 1946–47 shape the concerns of the framers?
steps: Partition violence made unity and order urgent.
Uncertainty over princely states raised fears of fragmentation.
Mass movements and the RIN mutiny showed popular demands for freedom and justice.
So the framers stressed unity, a strong centre and rights for all.
example.answer: They made the framers concerned with national unity, stability and protecting the rights of all citizens.
